title: Trillions of cells: your own cells, and the microbes who live with them

summary.text: Brush your teeth until they are clean, and eat nothing all night. By morning a soft coat is back on them. The coat is made of living bacteria, who divided again and again while you slept. In this unit your child stains that coat to see it, and counts how many doublings turn one cell into the 17 trillion cells of a ten-year-old. They learn how scientists count cells that nobody can count one by one, and how a wrong number, 'ten microbes for every human cell', lasted forty years. A body carries about as many microbe cells as cells of its own, and scientists still argue about whether that makes you one living being or many.
summary.art: A child looking into a bathroom mirror with a torch, her front teeth showing a thin line of red colour along the gums, and a small bottle of red food colour on the basin.

intro.hook: Tomorrow morning, before you brush, run your tongue slowly over your front teeth. They feel a little furry. Last night, after brushing, they felt smooth. You ate nothing while you slept. So what is the furry coat, and where did it come from?
intro.text: The coat is alive. It is made of bacteria, and each bacterium is one single cell. A few stayed on your teeth after brushing, and each of them divided into two, again and again, all night. Your own body is built in the same way, from cells who divide. It has about 17 trillion cells of its own, and about as many microbe cells live on it and in it. In this unit you make the coat on your teeth show up in colour, and you find out how anyone can count to a trillion.
intro.art: A sleepy child in pyjamas at a bathroom basin in the morning, touching her front teeth with the tip of her tongue, with a toothbrush still in the holder.

outcomes: I can say about how many cells are in my body, and explain how scientists estimate a number that is too big to count.
I can give evidence that each cell in my body is alive on her own.
I can explain that a body grows mainly by making more cells, and work out how doubling gets from one cell to trillions.
I can explain why a grown-up's body stays the same size while making billions of new cells every day.
I can say where the microbes on and in my body live, about how many there are, and what they and my body do for each other.
I can run a fair staining test on my own teeth, and explain what the result shows about living bacteria.
I can give two views on the question 'Am I one living being or many?', with evidence for each.
I can explain how the 'ten to one' number was shown to be wrong, and why a sample must be checked.

terms.meaning: A cell is the smallest part of a living thing that is alive on her own. She takes in food, uses energy, senses what is around her and can make new cells.
terms.example: A red blood cell, a skin cell and a bacterium are each one cell.
terms.art: A round animal cell with a thin skin and a nucleus, drawn next to a much smaller rod-shaped bacterium.

terms.meaning: A trillion is a million millions. It is written as 1 followed by 12 zeros. In the Indian system it is one lakh crore.
terms.example: A ten-year-old child is made of about 17 trillion cells, which is 17 lakh crore.
terms.art: The number 1,000,000,000,000 written large, with '1 lakh crore' written under it in a child's handwriting.

terms.meaning: An estimate is a careful answer that you work out when you cannot count or measure exactly. A good estimate says how it was worked out.
terms.example: 'About 17 trillion cells' is an estimate. Nobody counted them one by one.
terms.art: A child holding a tumbler of chana and writing 'about 350?' in a notebook.

terms.meaning: A sample is a small part that you count or measure, so that you can work out the whole.
terms.example: You count the chana in one spoonful. That spoonful is your sample of the whole tumbler.
terms.art: One level tablespoon of chana tipped onto a steel plate, next to a full tumbler of chana.

terms.meaning: A red blood cell is a small disc-shaped cell that carries oxygen in your blood. A grown red blood cell has no nucleus.
terms.example: More than 8 out of every 10 of your own cells are red blood cells.
terms.art: A stream of red disc-shaped cells with dimpled centres moving through a narrow tube.

terms.meaning: Cell division is how one cell becomes two. The cell copies her instructions and then splits into two cells.
terms.example: You grew from one cell to trillions of cells by cell division.
terms.art: One round cell pinching in the middle, then two round cells side by side.

terms.meaning: Doubling means becoming twice as many. When every cell in a group divides once, the number of cells doubles.
terms.example: 1 cell, then 2, then 4, then 8, then 16. That is four doublings.
terms.art: A row of dots growing from 1 to 2 to 4 to 8 to 16, joined by branching lines.

terms.meaning: Cell turnover is the body making new cells to take the place of cells that wear out and die.
terms.example: Your body makes about two and a half million new red blood cells every second, and loses about as many.
terms.art: Two arrows around a drop of blood, one labelled 'new cells in' and one labelled 'old cells out'.

terms.meaning: A capillary is the thinnest kind of blood tube. Its wall is one cell thick, so food and oxygen can pass through to the cells nearby.
terms.example: Press your fingernail and it goes pale, because you pushed the blood out of the capillaries under it.
terms.art: A very thin tube with red blood cells passing through in single file, and body cells packed close on both sides.

terms.meaning: A microbe is a living being too small to see with your eyes alone. Most microbes are a single cell.
terms.art: A drop of water with three kinds of tiny single cells in it: rods, balls and an oval yeast with a bud.

terms.meaning: A bacterium is a single-celled living being with no nucleus. Many are called bacteria. Most bacteria are about ten times smaller across than your own cells.
terms.example: The bacteria in curd turn milk sour and thick.
terms.art: A group of rod-shaped and ball-shaped bacteria next to a much larger human cheek cell, to show the difference in size.

terms.meaning: Your microbiome is all the microbes who live on your body and in it: bacteria, and also some fungi, viruses and other tiny beings.
terms.example: The bacteria in your gut, on your skin and on your teeth are all part of your microbiome.
terms.art: An outline of a child's body with coloured dots thick in the belly, the mouth and the armpits, and thin on the arms.

terms.meaning: The large intestine is the wide last part of your food tube. Food that your own body could not digest ends up there. Most of your microbes live in it.
terms.example: The fibre from a banana or from sambar vegetables reaches your large intestine, and bacteria there feed on it.
terms.art: A simple drawing of the food tube inside a body, with the wide last loop coloured and labelled 'large intestine'.

terms.meaning: Fibre is the part of plant food that your own body has no way to break down. Many gut bacteria can break it down.
terms.example: Whole ragi, dal, banana, guava and vegetables are rich in fibre.
terms.art: A banana-leaf plate with ragi mudde, dal, a guava and beans poriyal.

terms.meaning: Plaque is the soft, sticky coat that grows on teeth. It is made of living bacteria and the glue they make.
terms.example: The furry feeling on your teeth in the morning is plaque.
terms.art: A close view of two front teeth with a pale, soft layer along the gum line.

terms.meaning: A biofilm is a layer of microbes who stick to a surface and to each other, inside a slime that they make themselves.
terms.example: Plaque on teeth and the slippery layer inside a water bottle that is not washed are both biofilms.
terms.art: A side view of a surface with bacteria of several shapes packed in layers inside a clear slime.

terms.meaning: A germ-free animal is one that scientists have raised in a sealed, clean chamber with no microbes at all.
terms.example: Germ-free mice help scientists find out what microbes do for a body.
terms.art: A mouse inside a clear sealed chamber with long rubber gloves fixed into its wall.

terms.meaning: A micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre. Scientists use it to measure cells.
terms.example: A red blood cell is about 8 micrometres across. A bacterium is about 1 or 2.
terms.art: A ruler's one-millimetre gap zoomed in and divided into a thousand tiny parts, with a red blood cell covering eight of them.

explanations.concept: How many cells are in you
explanations.definition: A ten-year-old child is made of about 17 trillion cells. A grown-up is made of about 30 to 36 trillion. These numbers are estimates, not counts.
explanations.description: Nobody can count a trillion of anything one by one. If you counted one cell every second without stopping, 17 trillion cells would take more than 500,000 years. So scientists use samples. They take one kind of tissue, such as blood, liver or fat. They measure how much of it a body has, and how many cells are in one small measured piece. Then they multiply, and add up all the tissues. In 2013 Eva Bianconi and her team in Italy did this organ by organ and got about 37 trillion for a grown-up. In 2023 a team led by Ian Hatton used over 400 kinds of cell and got about 36 trillion for a man of 70 kilograms, 28 trillion for a woman of 60 kilograms and 17 trillion for a child of ten. The numbers differ because bodies differ in size, and because every sample has some error. That is normal for an estimate, and honest scientists say so.
examples: One drop of blood, the size of a pinhead, holds about 5 million red blood cells. Labs count a tiny measured sample and multiply.
In Count Without Counting, you count the chana in one spoonful and work out the tumbler. Scientists count cells in the same way.
17 trillion is 17,000,000,000,000. In the Indian system that is 17 lakh crore.
explanations.art: A child's outline filled with tiny dots, with a magnifying circle on one fingertip showing a small square of counted cells and a multiplication sign.

explanations.concept: Each of your cells is alive
explanations.definition: Every cell in your body is a living being. She takes in food and oxygen, releases energy, gets rid of waste, senses signals and answers them.
explanations.description: It is easy to think of cells as bricks, because pictures show them packed in rows. But a brick does nothing, and a cell is busy every second. How do we know each one is alive on her own? One piece of evidence is that cells taken from a body can go on living in a dish, if they are kept warm and fed. Heart muscle cells in a dish keep beating. Another piece of evidence is that some cells travel alone. A white blood cell called a neutrophil crawls between other cells. When she senses chemicals that bacteria give off, she turns and follows them, and swallows the bacterium when she catches up. David Rogers filmed this under a microscope in the 1950s. Cells sense and decide. Some scientists prefer to say that a cell only reacts to chemicals, and that 'decide' is too strong a word. Because each cell is alive, each one needs food and oxygen all the time. That is why thin blood tubes called capillaries run within about a hair's width of nearly every cell.
examples: Press on your thumbnail. The pink goes pale and comes back in about two seconds. That pink is blood on the way to feed living cells.
Sit on your foot for too long and it goes numb. Its nerve cells were squeezed and short of blood, and they stopped sending signals properly.
Skin cells from one person can be grown in a dish into sheets of new skin for burns.

perspectives.explanation: A cell senses chemicals with special parts on her skin, and those parts switch other parts on and off. The cell changes direction as a result. They describe this as a response, and many would not call it a decision.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study how cells behave, such as Dennis Bray
perspectives.explanation: A cell takes in many signals at once, weighs them and acts. That is what deciding means, even when it is done with chemicals and not with a brain.

explanations.art: A white blood cell with a wavy edge crawling between round red blood cells towards a small dark bacterium.

explanations.concept: The kinds of cells in you, by number
explanations.definition: Your body has several hundred kinds of cell. By number, most of them are red blood cells.
explanations.description: Ask most people which cells they have the most of, and they say skin or muscle. In fact about 84 out of every 100 of your own cells are red blood cells. They are very small, and there are about 5 million in a drop of blood the size of a pinhead. About 5 more in every 100 are platelets, which help blood to clot. Platelets are small pieces of a larger cell, with no nucleus, so some scientists do not count them as full cells. All your muscle cells, fat cells, nerve cells, skin cells and bone cells together make up only a few in every 100. Yet muscle and fat make up most of your weight, because each muscle cell or fat cell is thousands of times bigger than a red blood cell. Old books say there are about 200 kinds of cell. Newer studies read which instructions each cell is using, and they find many more kinds. Scientists do not yet agree on how different two cells must be to count as two kinds.
examples: A red blood cell is about 8 micrometres across. About 125 of them in a row would measure one millimetre.
A nerve cell that runs from the bottom of your spine to your big toe is one single cell, about as long as your leg.
A human egg cell is about a tenth of a millimetre across. It is one of the few human cells that sharp eyes can just see.
explanations.art: A pie chart drawn as a round plate, with a very large red slice labelled 'red blood cells' and a few thin slices labelled 'platelets' and 'all the rest'.

explanations.concept: A body grows by making more cells
explanations.definition: A living body grows bigger mainly by making more cells through cell division. The cells themselves stay about the same size.
explanations.description: You began as one cell, a fertilised egg. That cell divided into 2, the 2 into 4, the 4 into 8. This is called doubling. Doubling grows very fast. After 10 doublings there are about a thousand cells, after 20 about a million, after 30 about a billion, and after 40 about a trillion. Just 44 doublings would be enough to make 17 trillion. So why does growing up take years and not 44 days? Because real cells do not all keep dividing. Most cells take up a job, such as nerve or muscle, and then divide rarely or never. Many cells die and are replaced on the way. Each division also needs food to build the new cell from. How do we know that growing means more cells, and not bigger cells? Compare animals. A cell from a mouse, a human and an elephant are close to the same size. The elephant is bigger because she has far more cells. There are exceptions. Fat cells swell when they store more fat, and muscle cells grow thicker with exercise.
examples: A newborn baby has roughly one to two trillion cells, going by body weight. A ten-year-old has about 17 trillion.
In Count the Doublings, you double on a calculator until you pass 17 trillion, and count the steps.
A banyan grows from a seed smaller than a mustard seed to a tree that covers a field, by adding cells.
explanations.art: A branching drawing in which one cell becomes two, then four, then eight, with the bottom row fading into a crowd too large to draw.

explanations.concept: Staying the same size: new cells in, old cells out
explanations.definition: A grown body makes about 330 billion new cells every day and loses about the same number. So it stays the same size.
explanations.description: In 2021 Ron Sender and Ron Milo added up how fast each kind of cell is replaced. Their total was about 330 billion cells a day, or nearly 4 million every second. Most of these are blood cells and cells that line the gut. Why those? Red blood cells are squeezed through thin capillaries for about four months, with no nucleus to help them repair themselves, and they wear out. Gut lining cells are rubbed by food and bathed in strong juices, and they last only a few days. A growing child makes a little more than they lose, so the number of cells goes up. In a grown-up the two are equal. If a group of cells makes more than it should, the result is a lump, and some lumps are cancers. If the body makes too few red blood cells, the person becomes pale and tired. This is called anaemia, and it is common in India when food has too little iron. So a steady body is a balance that is kept up every second.
examples: The dust on a shelf at home is partly flakes of dead skin cells that people have shed.
A person who gives blood makes the red blood cells again within a few weeks.
Your fingernail grows about 3 millimetres a month, because cells at its root keep dividing.
explanations.art: A bucket with a tap running in at the top and a hole at the bottom, the water level steady, labelled 'new cells in' and 'old cells out'.

explanations.concept: The cells in you that are not yours
explanations.definition: A grown-up body carries about 38 trillion bacteria, which is about as many as its own cells. Together they weigh only about 200 grams.
explanations.description: These bacteria are not an illness. They live on every healthy person. Nearly all of them live in the large intestine, the last wide part of the food tube. The rest live on the skin, in the mouth and nose, and in a few other places. Blood, muscles and the brain normally have none. How can 38 trillion beings weigh only as much as a glass of water? Because a bacterium is about ten times smaller across than one of your cells. That makes her about a thousand times smaller in volume. Bacteria are not the only residents. Yeasts and other fungi live on you too, and so do other single-celled beings called archaea. There are also many viruses, most of which live on your bacteria and not on you. Tiny eight-legged mites live in the hair roots on almost every grown-up's face. The number of bacteria changes through the day. Each time a person passes stool, they lose a large share of their gut bacteria, and the rest multiply again.
examples: A piece of plaque the size of a pinhead holds about 100 million bacteria.
One teaspoon of fresh curd holds many millions of living bacteria. They pass through your gut, and a few kinds may stay for a while.
The smell of a sweaty shirt is made by skin bacteria feeding on sweat. Fresh sweat has almost no smell.
explanations.art: An outline of a body with a thick band of coloured dots in the large intestine, some in the mouth and on the skin, and none in the heart, muscles and brain.

explanations.concept: What your microbes do for you, and what you do for them
explanations.definition: Your body gives its microbes warmth, water and food. In return many of them digest food you cannot, make some vitamins, and keep harmful microbes out.
explanations.description: Your own cells make no tools for breaking down most plant fibre. Bacteria in the large intestine do. They break fibre into small molecules called short-chain fatty acids. The cells that line your large intestine take most of their energy from one of these. Gut bacteria also make part of the vitamin K that helps your blood to clot. On the skin and in the gut, the resident microbes take up the space and the food. A harmful microbe who arrives finds it hard to settle. How do we know all this? From germ-free mice, raised with no microbes at all. Such mice must eat more food to keep the same weight. Their defences against infection develop poorly, and they need extra vitamin K in their feed. The microbes are not doing us a kindness. They are feeding themselves, and what they leave over is useful to us. Some of the same bacteria cause illness if they get into the blood through a wound. So where a microbe is matters as much as who she is.
examples: A mother's milk contains special sugars that her baby has no way to digest. They feed helpful bacteria in the baby's gut.
After a course of antibiotic medicine, some people get a loose stomach, because many gut bacteria were killed along with the harmful ones.
Idli, dosa, curd, kanji and dhokla are made by microbes, and each brings living microbes or the things they made into your gut.
explanations.art: A cut-away view of the gut wall, with bacteria on the inside breaking long plant threads into small pieces that pass into the wall's cells.

explanations.definition: A baby has almost no microbes before birth. Microbes arrive during birth and in the first years, from the mother, the family, food and the places the child lives in.
explanations.description: The first microbes come from the mother during birth, from her skin and from her milk. More come from every person who holds the baby, from food, soil, pets and other children. By about three years old, a child's gut community looks much like a grown-up's. No two people carry exactly the same set. In 2010 Noah Fierer and his team swabbed computer keyboards. They could tell which person used which keyboard by matching the bacteria on the keys to the bacteria on the fingers. What you eat changes your community too. In 2019 a team at IISER Bhopal compared people in Bhopal and people in Kerala. The two groups ate different food, and they carried different gut bacteria. People who live in one home share more microbes with each other than with strangers. Whether a baby has any microbes at all before birth has been argued about. Most scientists now think that a healthy womb has none.
examples: Twins who grow up in one home have gut microbes that are more alike than those of two strangers, but they are never identical.
A dog who lives in a flat shares skin bacteria with the people there.
A child who moves from Chennai to Shillong and eats different food will slowly carry a somewhat different gut community.
explanations.art: A newborn baby held by her mother, with small coloured dots passing from the mother's skin, from milk, from a grandmother's hands and from a family dog.

explanations.concept: The coat on your teeth is a city of bacteria
explanations.definition: Plaque is a biofilm: layers of living bacteria stuck to the tooth and to each other, inside a glue that they make.
explanations.description: Within minutes of brushing, a thin film from your saliva covers each tooth. Within hours, bacteria from your saliva and tongue stick to that film. They divide, and each one's family spreads. Other kinds then stick to the first ones. By the next day there is a soft layer you can scrape off with a fingernail. If it stays for a week or two, minerals from saliva harden it into tartar, which only a dentist can remove. Where does the coat grow thickest? Along the gums and between the teeth, where the tongue, the cheeks and the brush reach least. Most plaque bacteria live quietly. The trouble begins when the coat is thick and gets sugar. Some of the bacteria turn sugar into acid, and the acid slowly dissolves the tooth under them. Brushing does not make a mouth free of bacteria, and it does not need to. It keeps the coat thin. In 1683 Antonie van Leeuwenhoek scraped the coat from his own teeth and looked at it through his lens. He saw tiny living beings moving in it, and wrote to the Royal Society in London about them. They were bacteria.
examples: In the Morning Coat test, the colour sticks to plaque and shows you where the coat has grown back.
The slippery layer inside a steel water bottle that is only rinsed is a biofilm too.
A neem or babool twig, a brush and a finger with tooth powder all work in the same way, by wiping the coat off.
explanations.art: A greatly enlarged side view of a tooth surface near the gum, with rod-shaped and ball-shaped bacteria stacked in a soft layer.

explanations.concept: Are you one living being or many?
explanations.description: You are built from cells who each live, and you carry about as many microbe cells as your own. So is a person one living being, or a community? Scientists and philosophers give different answers, and the evidence does not settle it.
examples: A lichen on a tree trunk looks like one being. It is a fungus and an alga, and often a yeast as well, living as one body.
A coral is an animal with algae living inside her cells. Without the algae she turns white and may starve.
A termite has no way to digest wood without the microbes in her gut.

perspectives.who: Lynn Margulis, and biologists who use her word 'holobiont'
perspectives.explanation: A body and all its microbes live, eat and fall ill together, so they should be studied as one unit. Even your own cells are a team, because the mitochondria in them began as bacteria.

perspectives.who: Biologists such as Nancy Moran and Daniel Sloan
perspectives.explanation: You are one organism who has many residents. Your own cells all carry the same instructions and come from one fertilised egg. The microbes have their own instructions and their own interests, and some harm you when they get the chance.

perspectives.who: Many doctors who study the body's defences
perspectives.explanation: The body treats its microbes as neighbours to be managed. It feeds them, keeps them on the surfaces, and attacks any that cross into the blood. That looks like a border between two sides who mostly get on.

explanations.art: A child's outline made of many small different figures: round cells, rod-shaped bacteria and a few yeasts, all inside one outline.

explanations.concept: Down to atoms, and out to the whole Earth
explanations.definition: One of your cells is built from about a hundred trillion atoms. On Earth as a whole, most living beings are single cells.
explanations.description: There are more atoms in one of your cells than there are cells in your whole body. Those atoms do not stay. The water, the food and the air you take in bring new atoms, and old ones leave in your breath, sweat and urine. So a cell is more like a pattern that is kept up than a fixed lump of matter. Now look outwards. Your body has about a hundred times as many cells as there are stars in our galaxy, the Milky Way. And you are one animal among many. Scientists estimate that the Earth holds about a million trillion trillion bacteria, which is 1 followed by 30 zeros. In 2018 Yinon Bar-On, Rob Phillips and Ron Milo worked out the weight of all life. All the bacteria on Earth together weigh about 35 times as much as all the animals together. Plants weigh the most of all. Life on Earth has been single cells for most of its history, and by number it still is.
examples: A teaspoon of good garden soil holds more bacteria than there are people in India.
A carbon atom in a cell of your fingertip may have been in a rice plant in Thanjavur last year, and in the air before that.
Bacteria live in hot springs, in Antarctic ice, in clouds and in rock deep under the sea floor.
explanations.art: A zoom drawing in three steps: the Earth, then a child standing on it, then one cell of her hand filled with tiny dots for atoms.

explanations.concept: Do your gut microbes change how you feel?
explanations.description: This is a new field, and scientists only have early ideas. Gut bacteria make chemicals, and some of these act on nerves. A long nerve, the vagus nerve, carries signals from the gut to the brain. In experiments, germ-free mice behave differently from ordinary mice, and they change when they are given microbes. In people, the evidence is much weaker. Some studies find that people with low mood carry a different mix of gut bacteria. But a low mood also changes what a person eats, so nobody can yet say which comes first. It is honest to say this: gut microbes may affect mood a little, and nobody knows how much.
examples: Many people feel their stomach tighten before an exam. That shows the brain signals the gut. The question is how much the gut and its microbes signal back.
Shops sell 'probiotic' drinks that promise a better mood. The evidence for such promises is weak so far.
explanations.art: A simple body outline with a dotted line running both ways between the brain and the gut, and a question mark beside it.

agreed.text: A human body is made of tens of trillions of cells, and every one of them came by division from one fertilised egg.
agreed.evidence: Estimates made in different ways, by Bianconi in 2013, Sender in 2016 and Hatton in 2023, all land between 28 and 37 trillion for a grown-up. Cell division has been watched directly since the 1850s.

agreed.text: Each cell is alive on her own.
agreed.evidence: Cells taken from a body go on feeding, moving and dividing in a dish. White blood cells have been filmed chasing bacteria.

agreed.text: By number, most of your own cells are red blood cells.
agreed.evidence: A measured drop of blood can be counted under a microscope or by a machine. Multiplying by the 5 litres of blood in a grown-up gives about 25 trillion.

agreed.text: A healthy grown-up carries about as many bacterial cells as human cells.
agreed.evidence: Sender, Fuchs and Milo (2016) multiplied the bacteria in a gram of gut contents by the measured amount the large intestine holds. They got about 38 trillion bacteria, beside 30 trillion human cells.

agreed.text: Gut microbes digest fibre that our own cells cannot, and animals with no microbes are less healthy.
agreed.evidence: Germ-free mice need more food to keep their weight, need added vitamin K and have weak defences against infection.

agreed.text: Plaque is made of living bacteria who multiply on the teeth.
agreed.evidence: Leeuwenhoek saw them moving in 1683. Dyes that stick to plaque show it growing back within a day of brushing.

challenging.claim: Microbe cells outnumber your own cells ten to one.
challenging.who: Many books, museums and news reports from 1977 to 2016
challenging.for: It came from a real calculation by Thomas Luckey in 1972, and it was repeated by many respected scientists.
challenging.against: The calculation treated the whole gut as if it were as crowded as the large intestine. When Sender, Fuchs and Milo used the measured size of the large intestine in 2016, the answer fell to about 38 trillion. That is close to one to one.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous number: that you carry ten microbe cells for each cell of your own.

challenging.claim: A clean body is a body with no bacteria on it.
challenging.for: Some bacteria do cause illness, and washing hands with soap before eating prevents a great deal of it.
challenging.against: No washing removes all bacteria, and the ones who live on healthy skin and in a healthy gut help to keep harmful ones out. Germ-free mice are less healthy than ordinary mice.
challenging.context: This card is about what 'clean' means, when bacteria live on every healthy person.

challenging.claim: Cells are the building blocks of the body, like bricks in a wall.
challenging.for: Cells are small units, and bodies are built up from them. Under a microscope, onion cells do look like a wall of bricks.
challenging.against: A brick is not alive and does nothing. A cell feeds, senses, answers signals and makes new cells. A body is closer to a town of living beings than to a wall.
challenging.context: This card is about a common picture in school books: the cell as a brick.

challenging.claim: Every cell in your body is replaced every seven years.
challenging.for: Many cells are replaced often. Gut lining cells last days, skin cells weeks and red blood cells about four months.
challenging.against: Jonas Frisen's team in Sweden, and others, dated cells using carbon atoms from atom bomb tests. Most nerve cells in the outer brain and the cells in the middle of the eye lens are as old as the person. Heart muscle cells are replaced very slowly.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular saying: that your whole body is new every seven years.

challenging.claim: A person and their microbes are one single living unit, a 'holobiont'.
challenging.for: The body and its microbes feed each other and fall ill together. Some animals, such as corals and termites, die without their microbes.
challenging.against: Human gut microbes can live in other people, and many are picked up from outside in each new life. They do not pass from parent to child as reliably as a body's own cells do. So other biologists say they are residents and not parts.
challenging.context: This card is about whether you and your microbes should count as one living being.

challenging.who: Some popular books and probiotic advertisements
challenging.for: Gut bacteria make chemicals that act on nerves, and germ-free mice behave differently from ordinary mice.
challenging.against: In people the studies are small and often disagree. Mood also changes eating, so it is hard to tell cause from effect. 'Control' is far stronger than the evidence.
challenging.context: This card is about a claim often seen in advertisements: that the bacteria in your gut decide how you feel.

big_questions.q: Your teeth were clean at night and coated by morning, with no food eaten. What were the bacteria on your teeth feeding on?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is always in your mouth, even when you sleep.

big_questions.q: Just 44 doublings can make 17 trillion cells. So why did growing to your size take ten years?
big_questions.hint: Do all cells keep dividing? What does each new cell have to be built from?

big_questions.q: Most of your own cells are red blood cells with no nucleus. Most of your weight is muscle and fat. Which are you 'mostly' made of?
big_questions.hint: Try answering once by counting and once by weighing.

big_questions.q: If about half the cells in your body are bacteria, what does the word 'my' mean in 'my body'?
big_questions.hint: Is a home only its walls, or also the family who live in it?

big_questions.q: A mother's milk contains sugars that feed the baby's gut bacteria and not the baby. Who is the milk for?
big_questions.hint: What happens to the baby if those bacteria do well?

big_questions.q: A number that was wrong, 'ten to one', was printed in good books for forty years. How can you tell a checked number from a repeated one?
big_questions.hint: What would you want to know about where a number came from?

big_questions.q: Cells from a baby can stay alive in the mother's body for many years after the birth. Is a mother partly her child?
big_questions.hint: Scientists found such cells in mothers 27 years after their sons were born.

big_questions.q: A white blood cell follows a bacterium, turns when she turns, and swallows her. What would you need to see to say the cell is choosing?
big_questions.hint: Could you design a test in which the cell must pick between two things?

story.title: The Jelly That Stayed Firm
story.note: A true story, with imagined details. Fanny Angelina Hesse (1850 to 1934), called Lina, was real. She worked without pay as her husband Walther's laboratory helper and drew his bacteria for his papers. In 1881 she suggested agar, which she knew from making jellies, for growing bacteria. She had learned of it from a Dutch neighbour in New York who had lived in Java. Robert Koch mentioned agar in one line of his 1882 paper and did not name her. Her grandson Wolfgang Hesse told the story later. The words spoken, the two plates on the window sill and the exact day are imagined. Accounts differ on whether the Hesses were in Berlin or at home in Saxony that summer.
text: In the summer of 1881, Lina Hesse worked in two kitchens. One was the family kitchen, where she cooked for her husband and their children. The other was her husband's laboratory, where she cooked for bacteria.
Walther Hesse was a doctor. He wanted to know what floats in the air of a schoolroom, a bedroom or a mine. He did not mean dust. He meant the living things in the air that are too small to see.

Lina's work in the laboratory had no name and no pay. She boiled the beef broth that the bacteria fed on. She washed the glass. And she drew what Walther saw through the microscope, with a pen fine enough to draw one bacterium at a time.

The trouble with bacteria was that nobody could count them. One bacterium is far too small to see. A thousand of them in a spoon of broth are still too small to see. The broth only turns cloudy when there are many millions, and by then every kind is mixed up with every other kind.

That winter, Walther had learned a new way from Dr Koch in Berlin. You stir gelatin into the warm broth and pour it onto a glass plate. It sets like a pudding. Then you leave the plate open to the air for a while, cover it, and wait.

'Each bacterium lands in one place,' Walther had told her. 'She cannot swim away, because the jelly holds her. So she divides where she is. One becomes two, two become four. In two days her family is a heap so big that you can see it. A dot.'
'One dot for each bacterium that landed,' said Lina.
'Yes. So we count the dots.'
Lina had liked that very much. You could not see one bacterium. But you could keep her in one place and wait, and she would grow into something you could see.
That was in winter. Now it was July, and the gelatin would not stay set.

By noon each day the laboratory was hot, and the plates began to run. The dots slid into each other. Walther held one up to the window. Yesterday he had counted forty dots on it. Today it was one grey puddle.
'And look at this one,' he said. 'It is not even warm here in the corner. But some of them eat the gelatin. They turn it to water all round themselves.'
Lina looked at the puddle for some time.

'Each dot was one family,' she said slowly, 'only because nobody could move. When the jelly melts, the families run together. Then you cannot tell one cell's children from another's. The firm ground is the whole trick.'
Walther nodded. He had known that already, and it did not help him.
Lina went back to the other kitchen to see to lunch. On the shelf by the window stood a row of her fruit jellies, red and gold, made the week before. The sun had been on them all morning.
She stopped with the spoon in her hand. The jellies stood up straight. They had not run.

She had made jellies and puddings this way since she was a girl in New York. A Dutch neighbour had shown her family how. The neighbour had lived for years in Java, where it is hot every day of the year, and where cooks set their sweets with a dried seaweed called agar-agar. Gelatin jelly would be soup by noon in Java. Agar jelly stands firm.
Lina carried a dish of red jelly into the laboratory and put it on the window sill, in full sun, next to a plate of gelatin.
'Wait an hour,' she said.
In an hour the gelatin had run to the edge of its plate. The red jelly had not changed at all.
'It sets firm, and it stays firm in the heat,' said Lina. 'And nothing has ever spoiled it by eating it, not that I have seen. Boil it into your broth in place of the gelatin.'

They tried it that afternoon. The agar melted only when the broth was near boiling. Then it set into a smooth, firm sheet as it cooled. They left the plates open to the air of the room for a quarter of an hour, and covered them.

Two days later, in the worst heat of the week, the plates were still firm. On each one sat small round dots, white and yellow and one pale pink. Every dot was separate from the others. Every dot stood where its first cell had landed.
Walther counted them. Lina drew them.

Walther wrote to Dr Koch about the new jelly. The next year, Koch printed his famous paper on the bacterium that causes tuberculosis. One short line in it says that agar can be used in place of gelatin. It does not say whose idea that was.
Lina never asked for her name to be added, and she was never paid. She went on drawing bacteria for Walther's papers for many years.

Today, laboratories all over the world still use her jelly. When a doctor in Chennai or Kochi wants to know which bacteria are living in a child's sore throat, a swab from the throat is wiped across a plate of agar. The next day there are dots. Each dot began as one living cell who stayed where she landed, and divided.
story.epiphany: One bacterium is far too small to see. But she is alive, and a living cell divides. If she is held in one place, with food, her family piles up around her until it makes a dot that anyone can see. Each dot stands for one cell who landed there. That is how people count living things that are too small to see: they keep each one still, and let her multiply. It only works on ground that stays firm, and Lina Hesse knew a jelly that did.
ask: Why does one dot on a firm jelly tell you that one living cell landed there?
Why would the counting fail if the cells could drift about in a liquid?
A grain of sand on the same jelly would never grow into a dot. What does that tell you about the difference between a grain and a cell?
The idea that solved the problem came from a kitchen, not from a laboratory. Where else might useful ideas for science come from?
Many hands help to make a discovery. Who do you think should be named?

games.title: The Big Number Line
games.context: This is a card game about very big and very small numbers in the living world. Each card names something that can be counted. You put the cards in a line from the smallest number to the biggest, and turn each card over to check.

printables.title: 18 number cards to cut out (the number is on the back)

items.f: The cells you were made of at the very start
items.b: 1. You began as one fertilised egg cell.

items.f: The doublings needed to get from 1 cell to 17 trillion cells
items.b: 44. Doubling grows very fast.

items.f: The days one red blood cell lives
items.b: About 120 days, which is four months.

items.f: The bones in a grown-up's body
The kinds of bacteria found in human mouths
items.b: About 700 kinds. One mouth holds a few hundred of them.

items.f: The grains of rice in a 1 kilogram bag
items.b: About 50,000. You can check this by counting a sample.

items.f: The red blood cells in a drop of blood the size of a pinhead
items.b: About 5 million, which is 50 lakh.

items.f: The bacteria in a bit of tooth plaque the size of a pinhead
items.b: About 100 million, which is 10 crore.

items.f: The people in India
items.b: More than 140 crore, which is 1.4 billion.

items.f: The people on Earth
items.b: About 800 crore, which is 8 billion.

items.f: The nerve cells in one human brain
items.b: About 86 billion, which is 8,600 crore. Suzana Herculano-Houzel's team counted them in 2009.

items.f: The new cells a grown-up's body makes in one day
items.b: About 330 billion, which is 33,000 crore.

items.f: The trees on Earth
items.b: About 3 trillion, which is 3 lakh crore.

items.f: The cells of your own in a ten-year-old's body
items.b: About 17 trillion, which is 17 lakh crore.

items.f: The bacteria living on and in one grown-up
items.b: About 38 trillion, which is 38 lakh crore.

items.f: The atoms in one human cell
items.b: About 100 trillion. One cell has more atoms than your body has cells.

items.f: The ants on Earth
items.b: About 20,000 trillion. A team counted samples from all over the world in 2022.

items.f: The bacteria on the whole Earth
items.b: About 1 followed by 30 zeros. That is a million trillion trillion.

printables.title: A score sheet: one row for each round, to write how many cards you placed wrongly

rules: Shuffle the cards and keep them flat on the table, with the words up. Nobody looks at the backs.
Take one card from the pile and turn it over, so its number shows. This card starts the line.
Each player takes 3 cards and lays them words up. The rest stay in the pile.
On your turn, choose one of your cards. Say where in the line its number belongs, and give a reason. Then turn it over.
If you were right, the card stays in the line. If you were wrong, move it to its right place and take a new card from the pile.
The first player with no cards left wins.
Playing alone: place all the cards one by one. Count your wrong placings, and try to beat that number next time.

setup.caption: 1. Keep the cards words up. Turn one over to start the line.

setup.art: A row of five cards on a table with numbers showing, from small to big, and a child holding a sixth card above a gap in the row.
setup.caption: 2. Say where your card belongs in the line, and why.

setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards. 2. Shuffle them and lay them words up. 3. Turn one over to start the line. 4. Each player takes 3 cards.
flow.say: Every card names something we can count. Some numbers are tiny and some are huge. We will put them in order.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Lay them words up. Turn one over to start. Take 3 cards each.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Big Number Line. Here you set out the cards and start the line.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. 2. Each player chooses a card, says where it goes and gives a reason. 3. Turn the card over to check. 4. Play until one player has no cards.
flow.say: Before you turn the card, tell me your reason. Is this thing smaller than a cell or bigger? Are there more of them than people on Earth?
flow.kid: Pick a card. Say where it goes and why. Turn it over. Were you right?

ask.q: Which is more, the people on Earth or the cells in your own body? How do you know?
good: The cells in my body. There are about 8 billion people, and I have about 17 trillion cells.
17 trillion is about two thousand times as many as 8 billion.

flow.parent: The reason matters more than the answer. A good reason compares the card with one already in the line. For example: 'Each grown-up has 38 trillion bacteria, so the whole Earth must have far more.'
flow.context: This is the main part of the Big Number Line. Here you place each card in the line and check it.

flow.do: 1. Read the finished line aloud from the smallest number to the biggest. 2. Ask which card surprised each player most. 3. Write down how many cards were placed wrongly.
flow.say: Let's read the whole line. Which number surprised you most? Which two cards are closest together?
flow.kid: Read the line from smallest to biggest. Which card surprised you most?

check.q: Which of these is the biggest number?
options: The people on Earth
The cells of your own in your body
The bacteria on and in one grown-up
check.why: One grown-up carries about 38 trillion bacteria. A ten-year-old has about 17 trillion cells of their own, and the Earth has about 8 billion people. Choosing 'people on Earth' usually means that billions and trillions feel the same. A trillion is a thousand billions.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Big Number Line. Here you read the finished line and talk about the surprises.

games.title: Mine, a Guest, or Not Alive?
games.context: This is a sorting game about what your body is made of. Each card names something that is in you or on you. You decide whether it is one of your own living cells, a living guest, or not alive. A few cards have no agreed answer, and you argue them.

printables.title: 18 body cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A red blood cell in your finger
items.b: My own living cell. She has no nucleus, but she is alive and carries oxygen.

items.f: A bacterium in the coat on your teeth
items.b: A living guest. She is a single cell with her own instructions.

items.f: The hard white enamel of a tooth
items.b: Not alive. Cells built it before the tooth came through, and it has no cells in it.

items.f: A hair, above the skin
items.b: Not alive. It is made of dead cells packed with a tough material. The root under the skin is alive.

items.f: A nerve cell in your brain
items.b: My own living cell. Most of them are as old as you are.

items.f: A yeast cell on your scalp
items.b: A living guest. Yeasts are single-celled fungi, and they live on everyone's skin.

items.f: A bacterium in your large intestine, breaking down fibre
items.b: A living guest. She feeds herself, and what she leaves over feeds your gut wall.

items.f: The white tip of a fingernail
items.b: Not alive. That is why cutting it does not hurt.

items.f: A white blood cell chasing a bacterium
items.b: My own living cell. She senses, follows and swallows.

items.f: A mite in a hair root on a grown-up's face
items.b: A living guest. She is an animal with eight legs, about a third of a millimetre long.

items.f: The water in your blood
items.b: Not alive. More than half of your body is water, and your cells live in it.

items.f: A flake of skin falling off your arm
items.b: Not alive now. It was one of your living cells a few weeks ago.

items.f: A piece of bone
items.b: Argue it. Bone is hard mineral, which is not alive, with living bone cells sitting inside it.

items.f: A mitochondrion inside a muscle cell
items.b: Argue it. It is part of your cell. But its ancestors were free bacteria, and it still has its own instructions.

items.f: A baby's cell still living in the mother's blood years later
items.b: Argue it. The cell is alive and it lives in her body, but it grew from the baby.

items.f: A cell of a kidney given by another person
items.b: Argue it. The cell is alive and works for the new body, but it carries another person's instructions.

items.f: A curd bacterium you swallowed at lunch
items.b: Argue it. She is a living guest, but she may only be passing through.

items.f: A virus resting inside one of your gut bacteria
items.b: Argue it. Scientists do not agree on whether a virus is alive at all.

rules: Lay the three labels in a row. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, words up.
On your turn, take the top card and read it aloud.
Put it under one label and give one reason.
Turn the card over. If your pile matches the back and you gave a reason, you score one point.
If the back says 'Argue it', any pile scores a point, as long as your reason uses a fact.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: sort all 18 cards and say each reason aloud. Try to score 15 or more.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards and the labels. 2. Lay the labels in a row. 3. Shuffle the cards and pile them words up.

flow.kid: Read a card. Is it alive now? Did it grow from your first cell? Choose a pile. Say why.

ask.q: A hair is part of you, but it is not alive. How can both be true?
good: Living cells in the root made it, and then those cells died and hardened.
It is something my cells built, like a shell.

flow.parent: The two questions sort most cards. The argue cards are the ones where the two answers pull apart, or where scientists themselves disagree. Let your child hold their own view if they give a reason.

flow.say: Look at the six argue cards. Choose one. Which pile would you put it in, and what is your best reason?
flow.kid: Count your points. Pick one argue card. Choose a pile for it. Give your best reason.

check.q: Which of these is one of your own living cells?
options: The tip of a fingernail
A red blood cell
A bacterium in your gut
check.why: A red blood cell is alive and grew from your own first cell. The nail tip is made of dead cells. The gut bacterium is alive, but she is a guest with her own instructions. Choosing the nail usually means thinking that every part of the body is alive.

flow.context: This is the last step of Mine, a Guest, or Not Alive? Here you count the points and argue one hard card.

experiments.title: The Morning Coat: how much of the bacteria coat on your teeth grows back in one night?
experiments.context: In this experiment you brush your teeth clean at bedtime and stain them with food colour to check. The next morning you stain them again. The colour sticks to the soft coat of bacteria, so it shows how much grew back in one night and where.
experiments.question: After you brush your teeth clean at night and eat nothing, how much of the bacteria coat is back by morning? Where on the teeth does it come back first?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Tomorrow morning, will your teeth take no colour, a thin line of colour, or a lot of colour? On which part of the teeth will the colour show first? Write both guesses, and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: the time since brushing. Use the same number of drops of colour in the same amount of water each time. Swish for 20 seconds each time and rinse once. Score the same 12 front teeth with the same rules, in the same light. After the clean start, take only water until the morning test.
results_table: Score at the clean start (0 to 3)

materials.item: liquid food colour, red or blue
a teaspoon and a small katori
coconut oil or lip balm, to keep the colour off the lips
a toothbrush and toothpaste
a mirror and a torch or a phone light
a tumbler of water for rinsing
an old towel, because food colour stains cloth
paper and colour pencils for two tooth charts
plaque disclosing tablets from a chemist, if you want a stronger colour (not needed)

experiments.safety: Use only colour that is sold for food. Spit it out and do not swallow it. It stains cloth and can stain a basin for a while, so rinse the basin at once. Lips and tongue may stay coloured for a few hours. A child who reacts to food colours should not do this test.

schedule.what: At bedtime: guess, brush, stain, score, then brush to a clean start. Only water until morning.
Before brushing and before breakfast: stain and score again, compare the two charts and explain.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 12 teeth and add up each column. Colour the two tooth charts. Then write three sentences: what I thought would happen, what I saw, and why I think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: total score for 12 front teeth, out of 36

setup.art: A child lifting her lip in front of a mirror with a torch, showing front teeth with a thin red line of colour along the gums.
setup.caption: 3. Look at your 12 front teeth. Darker patches show the bacteria coat.
