flow.do: 1. Put the food colour, teaspoon, katori, mirror and torch by the basin. 2. Draw a tooth chart: two rows of six tooth shapes. 3. Ask for the two guesses and the reasons. 4. Write them down.
flow.say: Tonight you will brush your teeth clean. How much colour will they take tomorrow morning? Where will it show first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Draw two rows of six teeth. Guess how much colour shows tomorrow. Guess where. Say why. Write it down.

good: No colour, because I brushed and I will not eat anything.
A little near the gums, because some bacteria are always left.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children say 'no colour, because I brushed and ate nothing'. That is a reasonable guess, and the test will answer it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Morning Coat test. Here you get ready and guess, before you stain your teeth.

flow.do: 1. Your child brushes for two minutes, as well as they can. 2. Rub a little coconut oil on their lips. 3. Mix 4 drops of food colour into 1 teaspoon of water. 4. Your child swishes it over their teeth for 20 seconds and spits. 5. They rinse once with plain water and spit.
flow.say: Brush as well as you can. Now swish the coloured water over every tooth for 20 seconds. Spit it all out. Do not swallow it.
flow.kid: Brush for two minutes. Oil your lips. Swish the coloured water for 20 seconds. Spit it out. Rinse once.
flow.parent: The oil keeps the colour off the lips. The tongue takes colour whatever you do, because its surface is rough. The colour fades from the tongue in a few hours.
flow.context: This step of the Morning Coat test is the first staining. You brush at bedtime and then colour your teeth.

flow.do: 1. Your child looks at their 12 front teeth in the mirror, with the torch. 2. They give each tooth a score from 0 to 3. 3. They shade the same places on the tooth chart. 4. Add up the 12 scores.
flow.say: Look for patches that are clearly darker. Score 0 for none. Score 1 for a thin line by the gum. Score 2 for up to half the tooth. Score 3 for more than half.
flow.kid: Look at each front tooth. Score it 0, 1, 2 or 3. Shade your chart to match. Add up the scores.
flow.parent: A very pale tint over a whole tooth is not plaque. The thin film from saliva takes a little colour too. Count only patches that are clearly darker. Most children find colour along the gums and between the teeth, even after careful brushing.
flow.context: This step of the Morning Coat test is the first scoring. It shows which places the brush missed.

flow.do: 1. Your child brushes again, aiming at the coloured places, until no dark patches are left. 2. Check in the mirror. 3. Write the clean start score, which should be 0 or close to it. 4. From now on, only water until morning.
flow.say: Now brush the coloured places away. This is our clean start. From now until morning, drink only water.
flow.kid: Brush the coloured places away. Check in the mirror. Write your clean start score. Only water until morning.
flow.wait: Leave it until tomorrow morning. Do the next step before brushing and before breakfast.
flow.context: This step of the Morning Coat test makes a clean start. You brush away everything the colour showed.

flow.do: 1. Before brushing or eating, your child feels their teeth with their tongue. 2. Oil the lips and mix fresh coloured water, exactly as before. 3. Swish for 20 seconds, spit and rinse once. 4. Score the same 12 teeth and shade a second chart.
flow.say: Before the colour, feel your teeth with your tongue. What do you notice? Now stain them exactly as you did last night, and score them.
flow.kid: Feel your teeth with your tongue. Stain them the same way as last night. Score the 12 teeth. Shade a new chart.
flow.parent: Expect colour along the gums and between the teeth. A total of 6 to 15 out of 36 is common, but any total is a real result. If no tooth shows any colour at all, the mix was probably too weak. Try again the next morning with 8 drops, or with a disclosing tablet.
flow.context: This step of the Morning Coat test is the morning staining. It shows how much of the coat grew back in one night.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two charts side by side. 2. Ask your child for three sentences: what I thought, what I saw, and why I think it happened. 3. Ask the two questions below. 4. Only then read the explanation of plaque together. 5. Your child brushes the colour away.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened. Where did the coat grow back first?
flow.kid: Put the charts side by side. Say what you thought. Say what you saw. Say why. Then brush the colour away.

ask.q: You ate nothing in the night. So where did the new coat come from?
good: A few bacteria were left on my teeth and tongue, and they divided.
They fed on things in my saliva.

ask.q: Why did the coat grow back first near the gums and between the teeth?
good: The brush and the tongue reach those places least, so more bacteria were left there.
Those places are sheltered, so nothing rubs the bacteria off.

flow.parent: Let your child finish their own explanation before you add anything. The idea to reach is that the coat is alive. A few bacteria stay in every mouth after brushing, and each one divides into two again and again.

check.q: In the Morning Coat test, clean teeth took colour again by morning, though no food was eaten. What explains this best?
options: Some colour was left from the night before
Bacteria left in the mouth divided in the night
Teeth make the coat by themselves
check.why: The clean start score showed that the old colour was gone. The coat is made of living bacteria. A few stay in every mouth after brushing, and each one divides into two again and again. Choosing 'teeth make the coat' usually means thinking of plaque as dirt, and not as living cells.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Morning Coat test. Here you compare the two charts and explain what you found.

experiments.title: Count Without Counting: can one spoonful tell you how many are in the whole tumbler?
experiments.context: Nobody has counted the cells in a body one by one. Scientists count a small sample and multiply. In this experiment you test that method on a tumbler of chana, where you can also count every one and see how close the method gets.
experiments.question: If you count the chana in one level spoon and multiply, how close do you get to the true number in the tumbler? What happens to the answer if the sample is taken carelessly?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many chana are in the full tumbler? Then guess how close the spoon method will get: within 10, within 50, or more than 50 away. Write both guesses and your reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Use the same spoon every time, and level it the same way, by sliding a finger across the top. Do not press the chana down. Take three samples and find the mean, because one spoonful can be a fluke. Fill the tumbler to the brim and level it in the same way.

materials.item: dry kabuli chana or rajma, enough to fill the tumbler (you can cook it afterwards)
a small steel tumbler, about 150 to 200 millilitres
a tablespoon, or the biggest spoon in the kitchen
a steel plate for counting on
a teaspoon and about a tumbler of uncooked rice, for the last step
a notebook and pencil, and a calculator if you like

schedule.what: Guess, count three sample spoons, measure the tumbler in spoons, estimate, then count every chana to check. Try a careless sample. Estimate the rice in a kilogram.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Write your estimate, the true count and the difference between them. Then write three sentences: what I thought would happen, what I saw, and why the method works.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: chana in a small tumbler
rows: Chana in one level spoon (mean of 3 tries)
Level spoons that fill the tumbler
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show how to set out your results. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A tablespoon heaped with chana, and a child's finger sliding across the top to make it level, with the extra chana falling back into a tumbler.
setup.caption: 1. Fill the spoon and slide a finger across the top to level it.

setup.art: One level spoonful of chana tipped onto a steel plate, with a child pushing them into groups of five with a fingertip.
setup.caption: 2. Count the chana in the spoon. Do this three times.

setup.art: A child tipping level spoons of chana into a small steel tumbler and making a tally mark on paper for each spoon.
setup.caption: 3. Count how many level spoons fill the tumbler.

setup.art: All the chana from the tumbler laid out on two plates in neat groups of ten, with a child counting the groups.
setup.caption: 4. Count every chana in groups of ten, to check your estimate.

flow.do: 1. Fill the tumbler with chana to the brim and level it. 2. Ask your child how many chana are in it, and why they think so. 3. Ask how close the spoon method will get. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: How many chana are in this tumbler? Do not count. Just look and guess. Why that number? And how close will one spoonful get us?
flow.kid: Fill the tumbler to the brim. Guess how many chana are in it. Say why. Write it down.

ask.q: How could we find out without counting every one?
good: Count a small part and multiply.
Count one spoon and see how many spoons fill the tumbler.

flow.context: This is the first step of Count Without Counting. Here you guess the number of chana before you measure anything.

flow.do: 1. Fill the spoon from the tumbler and level it with a finger. 2. Tip it onto a plate and count the chana. 3. Put them back and mix. 4. Do this three times. 5. Add the three counts and divide by 3 to find the mean.
flow.say: This spoonful is our sample. Level it the same way each time. Count it, put it back, and take a fresh one. We do three.
flow.kid: Level the spoon with a finger. Count the chana. Put them back. Do it three times. Find the mean.
flow.parent: The three counts will differ by one to four chana. That spread is worth noticing. It is the reason scientists never trust a single sample.
flow.context: This step of Count Without Counting takes the samples. You count one level spoon of chana, three times.

flow.do: 1. Empty the tumbler onto a plate. 2. Fill it again, one level spoon at a time, and tally each spoon. 3. If the last spoon is only part used, count it as a half. 4. Multiply the mean by the number of spoons.
flow.say: Now we need to know how many spoons make a tumbler. Tally each one. Then multiply. That is our estimate.
flow.kid: Fill the tumbler one level spoon at a time. Tally each spoon. Multiply your mean by the spoons.
flow.context: This step of Count Without Counting measures the tumbler in spoons. Then you multiply to get your estimate.

flow.do: 1. Tip the whole tumbler onto two plates. 2. Push the chana into groups of ten. 3. Count the groups, and add any left over. 4. Write the true count next to the estimate. 5. Subtract to find the difference.
flow.say: Now we do what scientists cannot do with cells. We count every single one. Make groups of ten, so you do not lose count.
flow.kid: Tip the chana onto plates. Make groups of ten. Count the groups. Write the true count. Find the difference.

ask.q: Was the estimate too high or too low? What might have caused that?
good: Too high, because my spoons were a bit heaped.
Too low, because I pressed the tumbler down but not the spoon.

flow.parent: Most families land within about one tenth of the true count. If your estimate is further out, look for the reason together. Was the spoon levelled the same way each time? Was the last spoon counted fairly?
flow.context: This step of Count Without Counting checks the estimate. You count every chana in the tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Take one heaped spoon of chana and count it. 2. Multiply by the same number of level spoons as before. 3. Compare this estimate with the true count. 4. Ask what went wrong.
flow.say: Now a careless sample. Count a heaped spoon, but multiply by the number of level spoons. How far out is the answer this time?
flow.kid: Count one heaped spoon. Multiply by your spoon tally. Compare with the true count. What went wrong?
flow.parent: A heaped spoon holds about one and a half times as much as a level one. So the estimate comes out about one and a half times too big. The famous 'ten to one' number for microbes went wrong in the same way. The sample was good, but it was multiplied by the wrong size.
flow.context: This step of Count Without Counting tries a careless sample. It shows how one wrong measurement spoils the whole estimate.

flow.do: 1. Count the rice grains in one level teaspoon. 2. A tumbler of 200 millilitres holds 40 teaspoons, and a kilogram of rice fills about 6 tumblers. 3. Multiply the grains by 40, then by 6. 4. Ask your child for their three sentences.
flow.say: Nobody would count a kilogram of rice. But now you trust the method. Count one teaspoon and multiply. Then tell me why the method works.
flow.kid: Count the rice in one level teaspoon. Multiply by 40. Multiply by 6. Say why the method works.

ask.q: Why does counting a small sample work?
good: Because the rest is like the sample, so each spoon holds about the same number.
It only works if the sample is fair and the multiplying is right.

flow.parent: A level teaspoon holds roughly 200 to 250 grains of rice, so a kilogram comes to about 50,000 or 60,000. Small-grained rice gives a bigger number. To count the teaspoon quickly, spread the grains and count in groups of ten.

check.q: Scientists say a ten-year-old has about 17 trillion cells. How did they get that number?
options: They counted every cell with a machine
They counted small samples and multiplied
They guessed, with no measuring
check.why: They measured how many cells are in a small piece of each tissue, and how much of that tissue a body has, and multiplied. Choosing 'they guessed' usually means thinking an estimate is the same as a guess. An estimate is worked out from measurements.

flow.context: This is the last step of Count Without Counting. Here you use the method on rice, which is too many to count.

activities.title: Pink Again: does blood reach a cold fingertip as fast as a warm one?
activities.context: Every cell in your body is alive, so every cell needs blood to bring food and oxygen. In this activity you press the blood out from under a fingernail and time how fast it comes back, first with a warm hand and then with a cold one.

materials.item: a mug of cold water, with ice if you have it
a mug of warm water, about as warm as bath water
a towel
a notebook and pencil

activities.safety: Use warm water that is comfortable to the hand, not hot. Keep the hand in cold water for one minute only.
activities.record: Write the seconds it took for the pink to come back in the warm hand and in the cold hand. Draw a fingertip and show where you think the blood goes.

setup.art: A child pressing firmly on her own thumbnail with the thumb of her other hand, the nail turned pale.
setup.caption: 1. Press on a fingernail for 5 seconds. It goes pale.

setup.art: The same thumbnail just after the press is let go, pale in the middle with pink returning from the edges.
setup.caption: 2. Let go and count how long the pink takes to come back.

setup.art: A child with one hand in a mug of water with ice cubes and the other hand in a mug of warm water.
setup.caption: 3. Cool one hand and warm the other for one minute, then test both.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses hard on one thumbnail for 5 seconds. 2. They let go and count the seconds until the nail is pink again. 3. Do it three times and write the times.
flow.say: Press your thumbnail until it goes pale. Let go, and count 'one-and-two-and'. How long until it is pink again? What do you think the pink is?
flow.kid: Press your thumbnail for 5 seconds. Let go. Count until it is pink again. Do it three times.
flow.parent: The pink usually returns in one to two seconds. It is blood flowing back into the capillaries, the thinnest blood tubes, under the nail.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pink Again. Here you press the blood out from under a nail and time its return.

flow.do: 1. Show the two mugs. 2. Ask whether a cold finger will turn pink faster, slower or the same as a warm one. 3. Ask for the reason and write it down.
flow.say: One hand will go in cold water and one in warm. Which thumbnail will turn pink again sooner? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which thumb turns pink sooner, the cold one or the warm one. Say why. Write it down.

good: The cold one is slower, because cold makes things slow down.
The same, because the heart pumps to both hands.

flow.context: This step of Pink Again is for guessing. You guess before you cool and warm your hands.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds one hand in the cold water and the other in the warm water for one minute. 2. Dry both hands quickly. 3. Press and time the cold thumbnail, then the warm one. 4. Write both times.
flow.say: Keep both hands in for one minute. Now dry them fast. Press each thumbnail for 5 seconds and count how long the pink takes.
flow.kid: Hold one hand in cold water and one in warm. Wait one minute. Dry them. Time each thumbnail.
flow.parent: The cold nail usually takes clearly longer, often three seconds or more. If you see no difference, the water was not cold enough. Add ice, or use water from the fridge.
flow.context: This step of Pink Again is the test. You time the return of the pink in a cold hand and a warm hand.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what they saw and why they think it happened. 2. Then explain what the skin does in the cold. 3. Your child draws a fingertip with its blood tubes.
flow.say: What did you see? Why do you think it happened? In the cold, the thin blood tubes in the skin become narrower. That saves heat for the rest of the body.
flow.kid: Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened. Draw a fingertip and its tiny blood tubes.
flow.parent: With narrower tubes, less blood reaches the fingertip, and its cells get less food and oxygen for a while. That is why very cold fingers become numb and clumsy. The cells are alive and they are short of supplies.

check.q: Why does every part of your body need blood to reach it?
options: Blood keeps the skin pink
Every cell is alive and needs food and oxygen
Blood holds the body together
check.why: Each cell is a living being who uses food and oxygen all the time. Blood brings both, through capillaries that pass close to nearly every cell. Choosing 'keeps the skin pink' names what we see, not what the blood is for.

flow.context: This is the last step of Pink Again. Here you explain why the cold finger turned pink more slowly.

activities.title: Count the Doublings: from one cell to seventeen trillion
activities.context: You began as one cell, and a ten-year-old has about 17 trillion. In this activity you double a number again and again, and count how many doublings it takes to pass 17 trillion.

materials.item: a phone calculator, or a pencil and plenty of paper
a notebook

activities.record: Write your guess and the true number of doublings. Copy the table of cells after 10, 20, 30, 40 and 44 doublings.

answer_chart.title: Cells after each number of doublings, starting from one cell

show.art: A phone calculator showing 1,024 and a notebook page with ten tally marks beside it.
show.caption: Double the number and make a tally mark each time.

setup.art: A notebook page with the numbers 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 written in a column, and a tally mark beside each one after the first.
setup.caption: 1. Start at 1. Double it, and make a tally mark for each doubling.

setup.art: A phone calculator showing 1,048,576 and a child's notebook with twenty tally marks in groups of five.
setup.caption: 2. Write the number down after 10, 20, 30 and 40 doublings.

setup.art: A notebook page with the number 17,592,186,044,416 circled and 44 tally marks counted beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Stop when you pass 17 trillion, and count your tally marks.

flow.do: 1. Write 17,000,000,000,000 at the top of a page. 2. Ask your child how many doublings it takes to get there from 1. 3. Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: You began as one cell. One becomes two, two become four. How many doublings until there are 17 trillion? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write 17 trillion with all its zeros. Guess how many doublings get there from 1. Say why.
flow.parent: Most people guess thousands or millions. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Doublings. Here you guess how many doublings make 17 trillion cells.

flow.do: 1. Enter 1 on the calculator. 2. Multiply by 2, and make a tally mark. 3. Keep going. Write the number down after 10 and after 20 doublings. 4. If the calculator runs out of room, use the short cut in the parent note. 5. Stop when the number passes 17 trillion.
flow.say: Each press is one round of cell division, and every cell divides once. Tally each press. Tell me when you pass a thousand, a million and a billion.
flow.kid: Enter 1. Multiply by 2 and make a tally mark. Keep going. Stop when you pass 17 trillion.
flow.parent: Short cut for a small calculator: after 20 doublings the number is about 1 million. Start again at 1 and call it '1 million'. After 20 more doublings you have about 1 million millions, which is 1 trillion. That is 40 doublings. Four more give 2, 4, 8 and 16 trillion, or 17.6 trillion exactly.
flow.context: This step of Count the Doublings is the doubling itself. You double a number and tally each doubling.

flow.do: 1. Count the tally marks. 2. Compare with the guess. 3. Ask the question below and let your child think aloud. 4. Read the explanation of growing together only after that.
flow.say: It took 44 doublings. If a cell divided once a day, that is 44 days. But you took ten years to reach this size. What could explain that?
flow.kid: Count your tally marks. Was your guess close? Why did growing take you ten years, not 44 days?

ask.q: Why did growing take years, when 44 doublings would be enough?
good: Not every cell keeps dividing. Many take up a job and stop.
Many cells die and have to be replaced.
Each new cell must be built from food, and that takes time.

flow.context: This step of Count the Doublings compares the sum with a real body. You ask why real growing is slower than doubling.

flow.do: 1. Your child copies the table of doublings into the notebook. 2. Ask the check question.
flow.say: Copy the table. Look at the jump from 40 doublings to 44. Four more doublings took us from 1 trillion to 17 trillion.
flow.kid: Copy the table into your notebook. Look at the last four doublings. How big was that jump?

check.q: After 10 doublings, one cell has become about a thousand cells. About how many are there after 20 doublings?
options: About two thousand
About twenty thousand
About a million
check.why: Ten more doublings multiply the number by about a thousand again. A thousand thousands is a million. Choosing 'two thousand' usually means adding where the cells are multiplying.

flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Doublings. Here you write down the pattern and check what it means.

activities.title: Where Would You Live? A microbe map of your own body
activities.context: Microbes live on and in every healthy body, but not evenly. In this activity you think like a bacterium who needs water, food, warmth and shelter. You map the damp, oily and dry places of your own skin, and mark where most of your microbes live.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper
colour pencils: blue, yellow, brown and red
two small pieces of thin tissue paper or newspaper
a mirror

activities.record: Keep the finished body map. Write one sentence on which guess was right and which one surprised you.

setup.art: A simple outline of a child's body drawn on a large sheet of paper, with colour pencils beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the outline of a body.

setup.art: A child pressing a small piece of thin tissue paper on her forehead with two fingers.
setup.caption: 2. Press tissue paper on your forehead and then on your forearm. Look for an oily mark.

setup.art: The body outline coloured blue in the armpits and between the toes, yellow on the forehead and nose, brown on the forearms and shins, and red in the mouth and belly.
setup.caption: 3. Colour the damp, oily and dry places, and the places inside.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a body outline. 2. Ask what a bacterium needs to live: water, food, warmth and shelter. 3. They mark three places where they expect the most microbes and three with the fewest. 4. They say why.
flow.say: Think like a bacterium. You need water, food, warmth and a place where nothing rubs you off. Where on a body would you settle? Where would you never settle? Why?
flow.kid: Draw a body outline. Mark three places with the most microbes. Mark three with the fewest. Say why.

ask.q: Why would a bacterium choose that place?
good: It is damp and warm there.
Nothing rubs it clean, and there is sweat or oil to feed on.

flow.context: This is the first step of Where Would You Live? Here you guess where microbes live on a body.

flow.do: 1. Your child presses a piece of tissue paper on their forehead for 10 seconds, and another on their forearm. 2. Hold both to the light and compare. 3. They feel which places on their body are damp. 4. Colour damp places blue, oily places yellow and dry places brown.
flow.say: Press the paper on your forehead, then a fresh piece on your arm. Hold them to the light. Which one has a see-through mark? What made it?
flow.kid: Press tissue on your forehead and on your arm. Compare them at the window. Colour damp, oily and dry places.
flow.parent: The forehead paper usually shows a see-through oily mark, and the forearm paper does not. Damp places are the armpits, the inside of the elbows, behind the knees and between the toes. Oily places are the forehead, the sides of the nose and the upper back. Forearms, shins and palms are dry. Just after a bath the oily mark may be faint.
flow.context: This step of Where Would You Live? tests your own skin. You find its oily, damp and dry places.

flow.do: 1. Your child colours the mouth and the large intestine red. 2. They write 'most of all' on the large intestine. 3. They write 'none, normally' on the heart, the muscles and the brain. 4. Compare the map with the first guesses.
flow.say: Now the inside. The mouth has many. The large intestine has more than everywhere else put together. Blood, muscles and the brain normally have none. How close were your guesses?
flow.kid: Colour the mouth and large intestine red. Write 'none' on the heart, muscles and brain. Check your guesses.
flow.parent: Damp skin carries many bacteria of a few kinds. Dry skin, such as the forearm, carries fewer bacteria but the most kinds. Julie Segre and Elizabeth Grice found this in 2009, by reading the instructions of bacteria from 20 places on the skin.
flow.context: This step of Where Would You Live? adds the inside of the body. You mark where most microbes live and where none do.

flow.do: 1. Ask the check question. 2. Your child writes one sentence on what surprised them.
flow.say: Which place surprised you? Why do you think the inside of the gut suits bacteria so well?
flow.kid: Write what surprised you. Why does the gut suit bacteria so well?

check.q: Where do most of the bacteria in a human body live?
options: On the hands
In the large intestine
In the blood
check.why: The large intestine is warm, wet and full of fibre that our own cells could not digest. Nearly all of a person's bacteria live there. Healthy blood has none. Choosing 'hands' usually comes from hearing about germs on hands, which matter for illness but are few in number.

flow.context: This is the last step of Where Would You Live? Here you say what the map shows.

activities.title: A Day as One Cell: a comic in six boxes
activities.context: Each cell in you is alive and has her own life: a birth, food, a job, neighbours and an end. In this activity you choose one cell, or one gut bacterium, and draw a day of her life as a comic.

materials.item: a sheet of paper folded into six boxes
a pencil and colour pencils

activities.record: Keep the comic. Under it, write one way in which the cell's life is like yours and one way in which it is different.

setup.art: A sheet of paper folded into six boxes, with small headings written in each box: born, food, sensing, job, neighbours, ending.
setup.caption: 1. Fold a sheet into six boxes and write a heading in each.

setup.art: A child drawing a round red blood cell with a small face squeezing through a narrow tube in the fourth box of a comic.
setup.caption: 2. Draw your cell in each box.

setup.art: A finished six-box comic about a white blood cell, held up by a child to show a parent.
setup.caption: 3. Read your comic aloud to someone.

flow.do: 1. Read the four fact lists in the parent note aloud. 2. Your child chooses one: a red blood cell, a white blood cell, a gut lining cell or a gut bacterium. 3. They fold a sheet into six boxes. 4. They write the six headings.
flow.say: Choose whose day you will draw. The headings are: where I was born, what I take in, what I sense, my job, my neighbours, how my life ends.
flow.kid: Choose one cell. Fold your paper into six boxes. Write a heading in each box.
flow.parent: Red blood cell: born in bone marrow. She pushes out her nucleus before she leaves. She takes in oxygen in the lungs, goes round the body about once a minute and lives about 120 days. The spleen and liver take her apart and the iron is used again. White blood cell (neutrophil): born in bone marrow. She lives about a day in the blood. She senses chemicals from bacteria, crawls after them and swallows them. Dead ones make up much of the pus in a wound. Gut lining cell: born at the bottom of a tiny pit in the gut wall. She moves up a finger-shaped fold over three to five days, taking in food, and is shed from the tip. Gut bacterium: she lives in the large intestine, without oxygen. She feeds on fibre and divides every few hours when food is plentiful. Many leave with the stool, and a large part of stool is bacteria.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Day as One Cell. Here you choose a cell and learn the facts of her life.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws one picture in each box. 2. They add one short sentence in the cell's own words under each picture.
flow.say: Draw what your cell would see and do. Under each picture, write one thing she might say. Keep to the facts you heard.
flow.kid: Draw one picture in each box. Write what your cell says under each one.

ask.q: What does your cell need from the rest of the body, and what does she give?
good: She needs food and oxygen from the blood.
She gives her work, such as carrying oxygen or taking in food.

flow.context: This is the main part of A Day as One Cell. Here you draw the six boxes of the comic.

flow.do: 1. Your child reads the comic aloud. 2. Ask the question below. 3. They write the two sentences under the comic.
flow.say: Read me your comic. In what way is her life like yours? In what way is it different?
flow.kid: Read your comic aloud. How is her life like yours? How is it different? Write both.

check.q: Which of these does a single cell in your body do?
options: Only sit still, like a brick
Take in food and answer signals
Wait for the brain to move it
check.why: Every living cell takes in food and oxygen, releases energy and answers signals from around her. Choosing the brick usually comes from pictures that show cells as a still pattern.

flow.context: This is the last step of A Day as One Cell. Here you share the comic and compare the cell's life with your own.

projects.title: The Nail March: how fast do your cells build a fingernail and a toenail?
projects.context: A nail grows because cells at its root keep dividing. In this project you paint a thin line at the base of a thumbnail and a big toenail. Over three weeks you measure how far each line moves, to find out how fast those cells are working.

materials.item: nail polish in a dark colour, or a fine nail file to scratch a line
a ruler marked in millimetres
a strip of white paper and a sharp pencil
a notebook

projects.safety: A grown-up paints the lines. Keep nail polish away from the eyes and mouth, and open it near a window.

schedule.what: Guess. Paint a thin line across the base of one thumbnail and one big toenail, touching the skin edge.
Measure the gap between the skin edge and each line. Touch up the line if it has worn.
Measure both gaps, work out the growth in a day, and explain.

projects.record: Make a table with four rows, for days 1, 8, 15 and 22, and a column each for the thumb and the toe. Draw a line graph with two lines. Write what you thought, what you saw and why.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand painting a thin dark line of nail polish across the base of a child's thumbnail, right against the skin edge.
setup.caption: 1. Paint a thin line across the base of the nail, touching the skin edge.

setup.art: A child's thumbnail a week later, with a small clear gap between the skin edge and the dark line, and a ruler held beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Each week, measure the gap between the skin edge and the line.

setup.art: A notebook with a small table of dates and millimetres, and a graph with two rising lines labelled thumb and toe.
setup.caption: 3. Write each measurement down and draw a graph.

flow.do: 1. Ask which will grow faster, the thumbnail or the big toenail, and why. 2. Paint a thin line across the base of one thumbnail, touching the skin edge. 3. Paint the same on one big toenail. 4. Let them dry. 5. Write the date and the guess.
flow.say: Which nail grows faster, do you think, the thumb or the big toe? Why? These lines will ride outwards as the nails grow.
flow.kid: Guess which nail grows faster. Say why. Get a line painted on a thumbnail and a toenail.
flow.parent: Make the line as thin as you can, and make sure it touches the skin at the base of the nail. If you have no nail polish, scratch a fine line with the corner of a nail file.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Nail March. Here you guess, and mark the two nails.

flow.do: 1. Lay the edge of the paper strip along the nail. 2. Mark the skin edge and the near edge of the line with the sharp pencil. 3. Measure between the marks with the ruler. 4. Do this for the thumb and the toe. 5. Touch up a worn line without moving it.
flow.say: The line has moved away from the skin. New nail has grown in behind it. Mark the gap on the paper strip and measure it.
flow.kid: Mark the gap on a paper strip. Measure it with the ruler. Do the thumb and the toe.
flow.parent: After one week the thumb gap is under a millimetre, so it is hard to read. That is fine. Write your best reading. The gaps are easier to read on days 15 and 22.
flow.context: This step of the Nail March is the first measurement, one week after marking.

flow.do: 1. Measure both gaps again in the same way. 2. Write them in the table. 3. Ask your child what they notice so far.
flow.say: Measure both gaps again. Which line has gone further? Is that what you guessed?
flow.kid: Measure both gaps again. Write them down. Which line has gone further?
flow.context: This step of the Nail March is the second measurement, two weeks after marking.

flow.do: 1. Measure both gaps. 2. Divide each gap by 21 to find the growth in one day. 3. Draw the line graph. 4. Ask for the three sentences. 5. Then read the parent note together.
flow.say: Measure for the last time. How far did each nail grow in 21 days? Say what you thought, what you saw, and why you think the two differ.
flow.kid: Measure both gaps. Draw your graph. Say what you thought, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A thumbnail usually grows about 2 millimetres in three weeks, and a big toenail about 1. Fingernails grow about twice as fast as toenails. Scientists are not sure why. One idea is that the hands get a better blood supply. Cells at the root of the nail divide, fill up with a tough material and die. So the nail you can see is made of dead cells.

check.q: A painted line on a nail moves away from the skin as weeks pass. What does that show?
options: The polish is sliding along the nail
New nail is made at the root and pushes the old nail out
The nail stretches like rubber
check.why: Cells at the root of the nail divide and add new nail behind the line, so the line is pushed outwards. The polish is stuck to the nail. Choosing 'stretches' usually means thinking that the whole nail grows, when only the root does.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Nail March. Here you take the final measurement and explain it.

challenges.title: Feed Every Cell: design the blood tubes for a patch of body
challenges.context: This is a design challenge on squared paper. Every cell is alive and must be next to a blood tube to be fed. But every square used for a tube is a square that cannot be a working cell. You design a network that feeds every cell with the fewest tube squares.
challenges.problem: On a grid of 9 squares by 9 squares, colour some squares red as blood tubes. Every other square is a cell, and each cell must share a side with a red square. Use as few red squares as you can.
constraints: All the red squares must join into one network, side to side, starting from the 'heart' square in the middle of the left edge.
A cell that only touches a red square at a corner is not fed.
Count your red squares. Fewer is better, because more squares are left to be working cells.
materials: a maths notebook with squared paper, or a ruler to draw the grids
a red pencil and an ordinary pencil
general: Stripes: colour rows 2, 5 and 8 red, and join them down the left edge. This feeds every cell and uses 31 red squares.
A comb: one red column down the middle, with red rows branching off it.
A spiral that winds in from the edge.
creative: Branch like a tree, as real blood tubes do: one thick trunk that splits into thinner and thinner twigs.
Add a few loops, so that there are two routes to each part. Real capillaries form a net with many loops.
Leave the tubes thin at the far ends and count how far each cell is from the heart. In a real body, no cell can be far along a blocked road.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own network. Can you feed all the cells with fewer than 31 red squares? Then block one red square and see how many cells lose their supply. Which design would you want in your own body, the smallest one or the safest one?

ask.q: Why can a body not simply fill itself with blood tubes?
good: Then there would be no room for the cells that do the work.
Tubes cost space and material, so a body builds just enough.

flow.do: 1. On the best design, cross out one red square as a blockage. 2. Your child finds the red squares now cut off from the heart. 3. They count the cells that have lost their supply. 4. They add a loop to the design and test the same blockage again.
flow.say: I am blocking this tube. Which tubes are cut off from the heart now? How many cells go hungry? Can a loop save them?
flow.kid: Cross out one red square. Find the tubes cut off from the heart. Count the hungry cells. Add a loop.
flow.parent: A design with no loops loses everything beyond the block. A loop costs extra red squares but keeps the cells fed. Real bodies pay that cost in most places.

check.q: Why do the thinnest blood tubes pass close to nearly every cell in your body?
options: Because every cell is alive and must be fed
Because blood needs to stay warm
Because cells are stuck to the tubes
check.why: Each cell uses food and oxygen all the time, and these can only travel a very short way out of a capillary. So no living cell can be far from one. Choosing 'stay warm' mixes up one job of the blood with the reason for the fine network.

worksheets.title: Trillions of cells and their guests (core)

items.p: About how many cells of their own does a ten-year-old have?
items.why: About 17 trillion, which is 17 lakh crore. Choosing a smaller number is common, because trillions are hard to picture.

items.p: True or false: scientists found the number of cells in a body by counting each one.
items.why: False. They count the cells in small samples of each tissue and multiply. The answer is an estimate.

items.p: A small part that you count, so that you can work out the whole, is called a ____.
items.why: A sample. In Count Without Counting, one level spoon of chana was the sample.

items.p: Which kind of cell do you have the most of, by number?
items.why: About 84 in every 100 of your own cells are red blood cells. Skin and muscle are what we see and feel, so they are common guesses.

items.p: Give one piece of evidence that a single cell in your body is alive.
items.a: Cells taken from a body can live, feed and divide in a dish. A white blood cell crawls after a bacterium and swallows her. Heart cells in a dish keep beating.
items.why: A strong answer names something the cell does on her own, such as feeding, moving, sensing or dividing.

items.p: True or false: a body grows mainly because its cells get bigger.
items.why: False. A body grows mainly by making more cells. A mouse cell and an elephant cell are close to the same size.

items.p: One cell divides again and again. Put the numbers of cells in order.
items.why: Each division doubles the number: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.

items.p: When every cell in a group divides once, the number of cells ____.
items.why: It doubles. This is why a few cells can become very many in a short time.

items.p: A grown-up makes about 330 billion new cells a day. Why does the body not keep getting bigger?
opts: About as many old cells die
The new cells are very small
The cells leave in the breath
items.why: The body loses about as many cells as it makes, so the total stays steady. Most of the turnover is blood cells and gut lining cells.

items.p: Sort each place by how many microbes normally live there.
items.why: Microbes live on the surfaces that meet the outside world, and most of all in the large intestine. The inside of a healthy body has none.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: Microbiome
all the microbes living on and in a body
Plaque
the soft coat of bacteria on teeth
Fibre
plant food that only gut microbes can break down
Capillary
the thinnest kind of blood tube
Estimate
an answer worked out from measurements

items.p: In the Morning Coat test, where does the colour usually show first?
opts: On the flat middle of each tooth
Along the gums and between teeth
items.why: The brush, tongue and cheeks reach the gum line and the gaps least, so more bacteria are left there to multiply.

items.p: Draw one front tooth the morning after brushing. Shade where the bacteria coat is thickest.
items.a: A tooth shape with shading in a band along the gum edge and up the two sides, and a clean middle.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the shading at the gum line and the sides. Shading the whole tooth evenly shows the coat as dirt that settles, and not as something that grows from sheltered places.
items.art: A large outline of one front tooth with the gum line drawn across its top.

items.p: Three of these are alive. Which one is not?
items.why: The tip of a nail is made of dead cells. The other three are living cells.

items.p: Name two things gut bacteria do that help your body.
items.a: They break down fibre that our own cells cannot digest. They make some vitamin K. They take up space and food, so harmful microbes find it hard to settle.
items.why: Any two of these are right. A strong answer says how we know, for example from germ-free mice.

worksheets.title: Doubling, turnover and the body's guests (stretch)

items.p: After 20 doublings, one cell has become about how many cells?
items.why: Ten doublings make about a thousand. Ten more multiply that by a thousand again, which is about a million. Choosing 40 means adding 2 each time, where the number doubles.

items.p: True or false: 44 doublings are enough to turn 1 cell into more than 17 trillion.
items.why: True. 2 multiplied by itself 44 times is about 17.6 trillion.

items.p: Just 44 doublings make 17 trillion cells. Give two reasons why growing still takes a child ten years.
items.a: Most cells stop dividing when they take up a job. Many cells die and must be replaced. Each new cell has to be built from food, which takes time.
items.why: A strong answer sees that real cells do not all keep dividing, so real growth is far slower than pure doubling.

items.p: A red blood cell lives for about ____ months.
items.why: About four months, or 120 days. She has no nucleus, so she has no way to repair herself, and she wears out.

items.p: Put these cells in order, from the shortest life to the longest.
a: A nerve cell in the outer brain
items.why: A gut lining cell lasts a few days, a red blood cell about four months, and most nerve cells of the outer brain last a lifetime.
items: A nerve cell in the outer brain

items.p: 38 trillion bacteria weigh only about 200 grams. Why so little?
opts: A bacterium is far smaller than a human cell
They live in the gut, so they float
Scales do not measure living things
items.why: A bacterium is about ten times smaller across than one of your cells. That makes her about a thousand times smaller in volume.

items.p: Sort each one: is it one of your own living cells, or a living guest?
items.why: Your own cells all grew from your first cell and share her instructions. Guests have instructions of their own.

items.p: Match each microbe home to what makes it a good home.
items.why: A microbe needs water, food, warmth and shelter. Each of these places offers some of them.
pairs: The large intestine
warm, wet and full of fibre
An armpit
damp, with sweat to feed on
The forehead
oily
The gum line of a tooth
sheltered from the brush and tongue

items.p: Label this body outline with three places where many microbes live and two where none normally live.
a: Many: the skin, most in damp places
None normally: the brain or the muscles
items.why: Microbes live on surfaces that meet the outside world. The gut is such a surface, because it is a tube that runs through the body.
items.art: A plain outline of a child's body with five blank label lines.

items.p: True or false: a perfectly healthy person has no bacteria in their mouth.
items.why: False. Every healthy mouth holds hundreds of kinds of bacteria. Brushing keeps the coat thin and does not remove them all.

items.p: In the Morning Coat test, why must you score the same 12 teeth with the same rules both times?
items.a: So that the only thing that changes is the time since brushing. If the teeth or the rules changed, a different score could come from that and not from the bacteria growing.
items.why: A strong answer names the one thing that is changed and says everything else is kept the same.

items.p: Two people talk about the bacteria on a child's skin.
items.a: A strong answer sides with the scientist, because bacteria live on all healthy skin and return after washing. It also grants that washing hands with soap before eating and after the toilet removes harmful microbes picked up from outside.
items.why: Both points can be true together. Washing matters for the harmful microbes we pick up, and the resident ones are part of healthy skin.

views.says: Our soap kills 99.9 percent of germs. Clean skin is skin with no bacteria.
Healthy skin always carries bacteria. They take up the space, so harmful ones find it hard to settle.

items.ask: Whose view fits the evidence better? Say when washing with soap really does matter.

items.p: Draw a bucket that stays half full while a tap runs into it. Label it to show cell turnover.
items.a: A bucket with a tap running in, labelled 'new cells made', and a hole or spout running out, labelled 'old cells lost'. The level is steady.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both flows at once. A bucket with only a tap would overflow, just as a body that only made cells would keep growing.
items.art: An empty outline of a bucket with a tap above it.

items.p: Three of these helped to show that 'ten microbes for each human cell' was wrong. Which one did not?
items.why: Repeating a number does not check it. The other three are what Rosner, Bianconi, Sender, Fuchs and Milo did.
opts: Measuring the large intestine's real size
Repeating the old number in more books
Checking where the number came from

items.p: A heaped spoon is counted, then multiplied by the number of level spoons. The estimate will be:
items.why: A heaped spoon holds more than a level one, so every spoon is counted as fuller than it was. The estimate comes out too big.

items.p: One spoon holds 27 chana, and 13 spoons fill a tumbler. Estimate the total. Why may it not be exact?
items.a: 27 multiplied by 13 is 351. It may not be exact because each spoonful differs by a few chana, and the last spoon may not have been full.
items.why: A strong answer gives the sum and at least one real source of error.

items.p: Two careful teams estimate a grown-up's cells as 30 trillion and 36 trillion. What is the best conclusion?
opts: The true number is near those values
items.why: Estimates made in different ways never agree exactly. When they land close together, we can trust the rough size. Choosing 'a mistake' treats an estimate as if it were an exact count.

items.p: True or false: most of your weight comes from the kind of cell you have most of.
items.why: False. Most of your cells are red blood cells, but most of your weight is muscle and fat. One muscle cell is thousands of times bigger than a red blood cell.

items.p: One human cell is built from about a hundred trillion ____.
items.why: Atoms. One cell has more atoms than your body has cells.

items.p: An elephant is far heavier than a person. Does she have bigger cells or more cells? How could you check?
items.a: More cells. You could look at a sample of her cells, such as blood, under a microscope and measure them. They are close to the size of ours.
items.why: A strong answer gives a way to test it, and does not only state the fact.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest number to the biggest.
items.why: About 8 billion people, 17 trillion cells, 38 trillion bacteria in one grown-up, and about 1 followed by 30 zeros bacteria on Earth.

items.p: Mice raised with no microbes at all need more food to keep their weight. What does that suggest?
opts: Microbes steal food from ordinary mice
Microbes help to get energy from food
Food is worse in clean cages
items.why: Gut microbes break down fibre that the mouse cannot digest, and the mouse takes in what they make. Without them, some of the food is wasted.

items.p: True or false: gut microbes help us because they want to be kind to us.
items.why: False, as far as anyone can tell. They feed themselves, and what they leave over is useful to us. Both sides gain, and neither has to intend it.

items.p: Two biologists disagree about what a person is.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence. For the first: germ-free animals are less healthy, and mitochondria were once bacteria. For the second: all our own cells share one set of instructions, and gut bacteria cause illness if they reach the blood.
items.why: Scientists have not settled this. The marks are for using evidence and for being fair to the other view.

views.says: A person and their microbes eat, live and fall ill together. They are one living unit.
A person is one organism. The microbes are residents with their own instructions and their own interests.

items.ask: Which view do you find stronger? Give one piece of evidence for it, and one fair point from the other side.

items.p: Mother's milk has sugars that only a baby's gut bacteria can use. What does that tell you?
items.a: A mother's body makes food for her baby's microbes as well as for her baby. So bodies have depended on their microbes for a very long time.
items.why: A strong answer sees that the body spends effort on feeding microbes, which only makes sense if they matter to the baby's health.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
items.why: Each of them found a way to see or count living things that are too small or too many to count directly.
pairs: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek
saw living bacteria from his own teeth
Lina Hesse
suggested a firm jelly for growing bacteria
Eva Bianconi
led a count of human cells, organ by organ
Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo
showed that 'ten to one' was wrong

items.p: Sort each statement: is it settled, or still argued about?
items.why: A claim is settled when different careful tests agree. The others have some evidence, but studies still disagree.
items: A grown-up carries about as many bacteria as human cells
Gut microbes change a person's mood
Cells come from other cells by division
A person and their microbes are one living unit
How many kinds of cell a body has

items.p: Draw one dot of bacteria on a jelly plate. Beside it, draw what it was two days earlier.
items.a: A round dot labelled 'millions of cells', and beside it a single tiny cell labelled 'one cell, too small to see'. An arrow joins them, marked 'divided again and again'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the visible dot is the family of one cell who stayed in one place and divided.
items.art: A round plate seen from above with one small dot on it, and an empty circle beside the plate.

items.p: The 'ten to one' estimate went wrong because a good sample was multiplied by the wrong ____.
items.why: The amount. The whole gut was treated as if it were as crowded as the large intestine, which holds much less.

items.p: A number is printed in many good books. What is the best reason to trust it?
opts: You can trace how it was measured
items.why: A number can be trusted when you can see how it was worked out and the working has been checked. 'Ten to one' was in many books and was still wrong.

quiz.p: How do scientists know roughly how many cells are in a body?
quiz.why: They measure the cells in small samples of each tissue and multiply by how much tissue there is. Choosing 'guess' mixes up a guess and an estimate.

quiz.p: Which is the best evidence that one cell is alive on her own?
opts: A cell can live and divide in a dish
quiz.why: A cell that feeds and divides away from the body is clearly alive on her own. Being small or having a skin is true of some non-living things too.

quiz.p: You have about 17 trillion cells. About how many doublings from one cell would make that many?
quiz.why: 44 doublings give about 17.6 trillion. Doubling grows very fast, so the number of doublings is small.

quiz.p: True or false: an elephant is bigger than a mouse mainly because her cells are bigger.
quiz.why: False. Their cells are close to the same size. The elephant has far more of them.

quiz.p: A grown-up's body makes billions of new cells every day. Which cells make up most of them?
opts: Blood cells and gut lining cells
quiz.why: Blood cells and gut lining cells wear out fastest, so they are replaced most. Most brain and heart cells stay for many years.

quiz.p: About how many bacteria does a grown-up carry, compared with their own cells?
quiz.why: About 38 trillion bacteria beside about 30 trillion human cells. 'Ten times as many' was believed for forty years and was shown wrong in 2016.

quiz.p: What do gut bacteria feed on that your own cells cannot digest?
quiz.why: Fibre from plants. The bacteria break it into small molecules, and some of these feed the cells of your gut wall.

quiz.p: Clean teeth took colour again after one night with no food. Why?
opts: The colour came back by itself
Teeth grow a new layer nightly
quiz.why: A few bacteria stay after any brushing. Each divides into two again and again, and by morning their families make a coat that takes the colour.

quiz.p: True or false: a body with no microbes at all would be healthier.
quiz.why: False. Germ-free mice need more food, need added vitamin K and fight infection poorly.

quiz.p: Which is a fair reason to say you are one organism and not a community?
opts: Your own cells share one set of instructions
Microbes are too small to matter
quiz.why: All your own cells came from one fertilised egg and carry the same instructions, and the microbes carry their own. This is evidence for one side of a real debate.

quiz.p: Why did the 'ten to one' number last for forty years?
opts: People repeated it without checking the working
quiz.why: The number was copied from book to book. When the working was checked, a wrong size for the gut was found. A number is only as good as its working.

applications: A blood test counts the cells in a tiny measured sample of blood and multiplies. A low red cell count shows anaemia, which is common in India.
Doctors grow bacteria from a throat swab on a plate of agar jelly, to find out which kind is causing an illness.
Dentists use a dye to show children where the coat on their teeth is thickest, so they know where to brush.
Sheets of skin grown from a person's own cells are used to treat large burns.
Doctors give antibiotic medicines with care, because they kill helpful gut bacteria along with harmful ones.
Makers of curd, idli batter and kanji depend on bacteria who multiply by dividing, just as cells in a body do.
Wildlife scientists count tigers, trees and fish by sampling, with the same reasoning as counting cells.

open_questions.q: Exactly how many kinds of cell are in a human body?
open_questions.why_open: New tools read which instructions each cell is using, and they keep finding new kinds. Scientists do not agree on how different two cells must be to count as two kinds.

open_questions.q: Is a person with their microbes one living being, or a host with many residents?
open_questions.why_open: The evidence fits both descriptions. It depends on what we decide the word 'individual' should mean, and scientists and philosophers disagree.

open_questions.q: Do gut microbes change how people feel and think?
open_questions.why_open: They do in mice. In people the studies are small and often disagree, and mood also changes what people eat.

open_questions.q: How does a body 'know' its right size, so that making cells and losing cells stay in balance?
open_questions.why_open: Cells signal to their neighbours, and some of the signals are known. Nobody can yet explain how trillions of cells keep the total so steady.

open_questions.q: Why do fingernails grow about twice as fast as toenails?
open_questions.why_open: Blood supply and how much the nail is knocked about may both matter. No test has settled it.

open_questions.q: Which of the thousands of kinds of microbe in us matter most for health?
open_questions.why_open: Most kinds have never been grown on their own in a laboratory, so nobody has studied what each one does.

How would you count the leaves on that neem tree without counting every one?
If a number is in a book, does that make it right? How could we check one?
When you say 'I am hungry', who is hungry: you, your cells, or your gut bacteria?

jokes.a: Twenty minutes later, there were two of her.

jokes.j: How many cells does it take to tell a joke?
jokes.a: About 17 trillion, and they all laugh together.

jokes.j: What did the red blood cell say on her 120th day?
jokes.a: I have been round the block a few times.

jokes.j: Why was the plaque bacterium up all night?
jokes.a: She had a lot of dividing to do before the morning brush.

jokes.j: What did the gut bacterium say when the fibre arrived?

jokes.j: Why did the white blood cell make a good detective?

jokes.j: What is a cell's favourite kind of maths?
jokes.a: Division. She uses it to multiply.

jokes.j: What did the toothbrush say to the bacteria?
jokes.a: Nothing personal. See you all tomorrow.

maths.problem: In Count the Doublings, 10 doublings turned 1 cell into 1,024 cells. Without doubling ten more times, work out about how many cells there are after 20 doublings.
maths.explain: Ten doublings multiply the number by 1,024. Ten more multiply it by 1,024 again. 1,024 x 1,024 = 1,048,576, which is about a million, or 10 lakh.
maths.context: This is about Count the Doublings, where you double a number again and again, as dividing cells do.
maths.why_maths: Seeing that ten doublings is 'times about a thousand' lets you jump ahead without pressing the calculator a thousand times.

maths.problem: A ten-year-old has about 17,000,000,000,000 cells. Write this number in words in the Indian system, using lakh and crore.
maths.explain: One crore is 1,00,00,000, which has 7 zeros. One lakh crore is 1 followed by 12 zeros, and that is a trillion. So 17 trillion is 17 lakh crore.
maths.context: This is about the number of cells in your own body, which scientists estimate at about 17 trillion for a ten-year-old.
maths.why_maths: A number with twelve zeros is hard to read aloud. Lakh and crore let you say it in three words.

maths.problem: In Count Without Counting, Kavya's three sample spoons held 26, 29 and 26 chana. 13 spoons filled the tumbler. Her true count was 338. How far out was her estimate, and is that within one tenth of the true count?
maths.answer: Her estimate was 351. It was 13 too many, which is well within one tenth.
maths.explain: The mean of 26, 29 and 26 is 81 ÷ 3 = 27. The estimate is 27 x 13 = 351. The difference is 351 - 338 = 13. One tenth of 338 is about 34, and 13 is less than 34.
maths.context: This is about Count Without Counting, where you count one level spoon of chana and multiply to estimate a whole tumbler.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the difference with one tenth of the true count tells you how good the estimate is, whatever the size of the tumbler.

maths.problem: A grown-up's body makes about 4 million new cells every second. About how many is that in one minute? Give the answer in crore.
maths.explain: 4 million x 60 seconds = 240 million. One crore is 10 million, so 240 million is 24 crore. A grown-up makes more new cells in one minute than there are people in most countries.
maths.context: This is about cell turnover. The body makes new cells all the time, to replace the ones that wear out.
maths.why_maths: A rate for one second is hard to picture. Multiplying it up to a minute lets you compare it with numbers you know, such as the people in a country.

maths.problem: A human cell is about 10 micrometres across. A bacterium is about 1 micrometre across. Think of both as small cubes. How many bacteria would fill the space of one human cell?
maths.explain: Ten bacteria fit along one edge of the cell. Ten rows fit across, and ten layers fit upwards. 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000. This is why 38 trillion bacteria weigh only about 200 grams.
maths.context: This is about why the bacteria in a body weigh so little, though there are as many of them as there are human cells. In Where Would You Live? you mapped where they are.
maths.why_maths: Something ten times smaller across is a thousand times smaller in volume. Working that out explains a result that looks impossible at first.

maths.problem: In the Morning Coat test, Meenakshi's total score was 0 at the clean start and 12 after 8 hours of sleep. If the coat kept growing at the same speed, what would her score be after 24 hours? Why can the real score never pass 36?
maths.answer: 36 by this pattern. It can never pass 36, because 12 teeth with a top score of 3 each make 36.
maths.explain: 12 points in 8 hours is 12 points for each 8 hours. 24 hours is three lots of 8 hours, so 3 x 12 = 36. The scale stops at 36. A real coat also slows down as it runs out of free tooth surface, so the pattern will not hold exactly.
maths.context: This is about the Morning Coat test, where food colour shows the coat of bacteria on 12 front teeth, scored from 0 to 3 each.
maths.why_maths: Carrying a pattern forward gives a prediction you can test. Seeing where the pattern must break tells you something about the scale and about real growth.

maths.problem: In the Nail March, a line on Arjun's thumbnail moved 2 millimetres in 21 days. His whole thumbnail is 12 millimetres long. About how long does it take to grow a whole new thumbnail?
maths.answer: About 126 days, which is about four months.
maths.explain: 2 millimetres take 21 days. 12 millimetres is 6 times as much, so it takes 6 x 21 = 126 days. That is a little over four months.
maths.context: This is about the Nail March, where a painted line shows how fast the cells at the root of a nail build new nail.
maths.why_maths: A small measured change, scaled up, tells you about a long process that you would not have the patience to watch.

how_we_found_out.context: This card tells how scientists counted the microbes in a human body, and how a wrong answer was repeated for about forty years.
how_we_found_out.story: In 1972 an American scientist, Thomas Luckey, wanted to know how many bacteria live in a person. He could not count them, so he estimated. One gram of gut contents holds about 100 billion bacteria. He took the gut to hold about 1,000 grams. That gave 100 trillion bacteria. In 1977 Dwayne Savage set this beside a rough figure of 10 trillion human cells. So people said that microbes outnumber our own cells ten to one. The number was printed in books and shown in museums for about forty years. Hardly anyone checked where it came from. In 2014 Judah Rosner wrote that the number was very rough. In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo in Israel worked it out again. Only the large intestine is that crowded, and it holds about 400 grams, not 1,000. They also counted human cells again and got about 30 trillion. Eva Bianconi's team in Italy had got 37 trillion in 2013. The new answer was about 38 trillion bacteria to 30 trillion human cells. That is close to one to one.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Luckey and Dwayne Savage, who made and spread the first estimate. Eva Bianconi and her team, who counted human cells organ by organ. Judah Rosner, who questioned the number. Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo, who worked it out again.
how_we_found_out.when: The first estimate was made in 1972 and became 'ten to one' in 1977. It was corrected in 2016.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that a body has ten microbe cells for every cell of its own. The sample was fine, but it was multiplied by the wrong amount. When the true size of the large intestine was used, the answer fell to about one to one.
how_we_found_out.art: Two balance scales side by side: an old one tipped far down on the side marked 'microbes', and a new one almost level between 'microbes' and 'human cells'.

roots.context: In the Morning Coat test, the bacteria on your teeth grew back in one night. You have learned that your body carries about as many microbe cells as cells of its own. Now we ask what that tells us about who 'you' are.

deep_truth.truth: In the Morning Coat test, you brushed your teeth clean and the bacteria coat was back by morning. A grown-up carries about 38 trillion bacteria beside 30 trillion human cells. Mice raised with no microbes at all are weaker, not healthier. So your microbes are not dirt sitting on your body. They are part of how a healthy body works.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'my body' as if it were made only of our own cells. We call the microbes on it germs or dirt, as if a perfectly clean body would have none. The science shows that a body with no microbes works worse.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Morning Coat test the coat came back in one night, though you ate nothing. Sender, Fuchs and Milo counted about as many bacterial cells as human cells in a grown-up. Germ-free mice need more food, need added vitamin K and fight infection poorly. If your teeth showed no colour in the morning, write that down as it is and test again with stronger colour.

three.who_am_i: You are about 17 trillion living cells who all came from one cell. You are also home to trillions of smaller living beings who joined you after you were born. When you say 'I', all of them are included.
three.what_is_life: A living being is hardly ever alone in her body. Almost every animal and plant is also a home and a food supply for other beings, and many would not survive without them.
three.what_is_this_world: Your microbes came from your mother, your family, your food and the soil. So some of the world outside you now lives inside you, and does part of your body's work.

roots.thread: You began as one cell. That cell became many cells, and the many became different from each other: blood, bone, nerve and skin. Then other beings moved in, and your body became a community. Go back far enough and your cells and your bacteria are relatives. All life on Earth comes from the same first cells, more than three and a half billion years ago. One line of their children became bacteria, and another line, much later, became animals. In you, the two lines live together again. This is what the One becoming many looks like in a body: one cell becomes many cells, and one family of life becomes many kinds who still depend on each other.

science.text: A healthy grown-up carries about as many bacterial cells as human cells.
The mitochondria inside your own cells began as free-living bacteria, so even one human cell is a partnership.
Some biologists say a body and its microbes should count as one living unit, a holobiont. Others say they are one host and many residents.
Whether a community of cells has one awareness, or many, or how awareness arises at all. Nobody knows.

other_view.who: Many biologists, such as Nancy Moran and Daniel Sloan
other_view.view: You are one organism. All your own cells carry the same instructions and came from one fertilised egg. Your microbes carry their own instructions, come from outside, and would harm you if they got into your blood. They are neighbours you live well with. They are not part of you.

practice.title: One breath for everyone
practice.say: Sit still and put one hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly and feel your hand rise. The oxygen in this breath is on its way to every one of your cells. Breathe out. Now think of your last meal. Part of it is feeding your cells, and part of it is feeding the bacteria under your hand. Take five slow breaths. On each one, ask yourself quietly: who is this breath for?
practice.kid: Sit still. Put a hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly and feel your hand rise. This breath feeds all your cells. Your last meal feeds your gut bacteria too. Take five slow breaths. Ask yourself: who is this breath for?

ask: If your microbes help to keep you well, are they part of you, or are they someone else?

A cell in your finger and a bacterium in your gut share an ancestor from billions of years ago. What do you think about living together with such distant relatives?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this unit were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat the amounts as a starting point. The Morning Coat test (the core investigation) needs liquid food colour, a mirror and a torch. It takes about 26 minutes at bedtime and 14 minutes the next morning. Food colour stains cloth and can mark a basin, so put an old towel round the shoulders and rinse the basin at once. Lips and tongue may stay coloured for a few hours, so choose a night before a day at home. Kitchen food colour gives a weaker stain than a dentist's disclosing tablet. A pale tint over a whole tooth is the saliva film and does not count. If nothing shows in the morning, use 8 drops, or the tablets. Score only the 12 front teeth, because back teeth are hard to see in a mirror. Count Without Counting needs kabuli chana or rajma, which can be cooked afterwards. Counting the whole tumbler takes about six minutes in groups of ten. Count the Doublings needs a phone calculator. A small pocket calculator runs out of room after about 26 doublings, and the step gives a short cut. In Pink Again the cold water must be really cold, or the two thumbs will look the same. In Where Would You Live? the oily mark from the forehead is faint just after a bath. The Nail March runs for three weeks. Nail polish wears off, so touch it up without moving the line, and expect the first week's gap to be too small to read well. In Feed Every Cell, the stripes design was checked: it uses 31 red squares on a 9 by 9 grid. We have not worked out the smallest possible number. Both games can be played alone. No part needs a garden. Facts checked against the papers named in the sources: the cell counts for a man, a woman and a ten-year-old, the 38 trillion bacteria, the 330 billion cells replaced each day and the history of 'ten to one'. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel but not watched. Things a person should check: the counts on the Big Number Line cards are all estimates, the Bhopal and Kerala study is described from memory of the paper, and accounts differ on where the Hesses were in the summer of 1881.
